speechtext:
It seems to me that this should be a question to the ministry when the orders of the day are called, rather than a question of privilege. Probably the misunderstanding has arisen because of the procedure I permitted at the last session, and for which I must take the responsibility. At that time there was no committee of supply and no committee of ways and means, and I allowed considerable latitude in raising questions of privilege and other matters at the opening of the sitting. I do not think, however, that I should follow that procedure at this session.
In my view we should abide by the rules in this respect, because under those rules there are ample opportunities to ask questions of the ministry and to bring up such matters as the one now indicated by the leader of the opposition. subtopic: PROCEDURE IN RAISING QUESTIONS OF PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
Naturally I am in no way questioning the statement you have made, Mr. Speaker. I would point out, however, that I raised the question at this stage because of the practice which, so far as I know, has been followed ever since my coming to the house-which is not so long ago. That practice has been that ministers and others have dealt with questions of privilege at the opening of the proceedings. So long as we understand that any questions raised by way of privilege or having to do with important public business are to be raised when the orders of the day are called, at the same time as questions are asked of the government, then I think all of us will very naturally follow the same pattern. I assume we may accept the statement you have now made, sir, as settling the procedure in connection with matters of this kind; that
such questions, whether raised by ministers or others, will be dealt with when the orders of the day are called instead of at the opening of the proceedings.

In the normal proceedings of the house there are opportunities afforded hon. members to raise important questions. At the present time the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is in progress, and in that debate important questions can be discussed. When the address has been adopted, I should think it is likely that there would be a committee of supply and a committee of ways and means; on the motion to go into committee these matters can be discussed.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. 8, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
When hon. members see the bill they will find that the preamble is in the same form as were the preambles to the bills which became chapter 54 of the statutes of 1933 and chapter 71 of the statutes of 1947. They will find that the statute recites that the results of the last census require, according to the constitution, that there be a redistribution of representation in this house. This is a duty imposed, not upon the government but upon parliament. I understand that the practice since confederation has been for the leader of the majority party in the house to take the initiative in bringing before the house a bill to carry out that constitutional obligation. This bill has been drawn in the form which has been in use as far back as I have been able to go.
It provides for the distribution among the provinces of the number of representatives provided by the rules fixed in the constitution. The representation within the provinces will be by electoral districts according to schedule. In accordance with the time-honoured practice the bill simply provides for the schedule and will leave it to a select committee of the house to draft the appropriate schedule.

The bill is being brought in at this time because it is felt, as it always has been felt, that it is a responsibility of parliament to deal with this matter immediately after the results of a census become known. This was felt to be such an obligation that even during the war, when there was a general feeling that it would not be proper to indulge in the controversies that sometimes arise over this matter, an amendment to the constitution was sought to authorize parliament to postpone until after the cessation of hostilities the consideration of a redistribution bill.
The bill is always brought down in the name of the government, but I feel it is more my responsibility as leader of the majority party in the house than as Prime Minister to introduce it, because it is not a matter for the executive government; it is a responsibility put upon parliament to determine something which is of particular concern to parliament.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ADDRESS BY MR. PEARSON IN NEW YORK ON  PROCEDURE IN RAISING QUESTIONS OF PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to refer now to the matter I mentioned before, but before I do so I should like to make one or two observations. Rulings become precedents and there are certain traditional procedures in this house which each one of us should understand. I have been under -the impression that it has been the practice to deal with matters of privilege at some stage before the orders of the day, and I am raising a question of privilege on this occasion for that reason.
Because of a remark which you made, sir, I would ask that you bear in mind that there may be many occasions on which debates would not be in progress which would permit the raising of some question. Unless the practice is continued, which has certainly been in force since I came into this house, of permitting questions of privilege to be raised as they have been in the past, it will be very difficult to discuss important questions of privilege, and I submit that any ruling now made should be made with the recognition of the fact that such a ruling would become a precedent which would have a substantial effect on the proceedings day by day in this house. I mentioned before that, as a matter of privilege affecting every member of the house, I wished to comment on the speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in New York on Friday, which was very extensively reported in the press of Canada. I do so for this reason. In the speech delivered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs he dealt with extremely important subjects connected with Canada's foreign policy. It has been indicated that we are awaiting with interest an opportunity to debate a resolution which will ask approval of the government's proposals that may emerge from the NATO conference at Lisbon and such other proposals as they may put forward with respect to the foreign policy of Canada.
At the very time that we are waiting for such an opportunity to hear a report we read in the press statements announcing new policies on which this house has at no time passed. The question whether we agree or disagree with those policies is not the point which should concern us. It is the authority of parliament itself over its own affairs, and particularly over such vitally important matters as the foreign policy of Canada at the present time.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Without enlarging too extensively on what was said, I should simply like to refer to one paragraph in the -speech made in New York on Friday containing four positive declarations of policy which I submit have not been passed on by the house. I shall quote not only from the press report but also from the text of the speech which was handed out by the Department of External Affairs. It reads as follows:
As for China, we should let the Peking government know that they must expect communist aggression to be met by collective resistance; that no government in Peking committing such aggression can hope to be accepted into the community of nations; that, on the other hand, we ourselves did not intervene in Korea, or, indeed, in Formosa in order to overthrow by force the government in Peking. I think also that we should make it clear that while Formosa cannot be allowed to fall into Chinese communist hands while aggressive war is going on in Korea, we do not intend to use our own forces to restore to China the regime which is now in Formosa after being driven off the mainland.
I would point out first that thi-s is a clear declaration that the nations, presumably the United Nations, should tell communist China the west's stand on aggression, and should tell China that any aggression will be met by collective action. This of course could have no meaning unless it referred to aggression by China anywhere in Asia, because already their aggressive action in Korea has been effectively resisted, and Canadians -are taking part in that collective action against aggression.
In the past the Secretary of State for External Affairs has very strongly resisted the suggestion that we should enter into a Pacific pact, on the ground, as I believe it was understood in the house, that our main concern was Europe and that no such general undertaking in Asia was appropriate at this time. Whether or not we agree, that certainly would appear to be the interpretation to be taken from reading the statements in Hansard on policy relating to this subject.
The next point that was clearly put forward was that no government in Peking committing aggression can hope to be taken into the community of nations. I for one would welcome unqualified assurance to that effect. It happens it is not the position that has been taken by the government of the United Kingdom, while on the other hand it is the position that has been taken by the government of the United States. Nevertheless, no matter what the individual point of view of any one of us may be, it seems to me that this is the place where a decision of that kind should be made.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I would merely make the comment that the reference to Formosa leaves the impression that we are engaged in the defence of Formosa. I was unaware of that.
I pass to the next point, namely, that we should make it clear that, while Formosa cannot be allowed to fall into Chinese communist hands while an aggressive war is going on in Korea, we do not intend to use our forces to restore to China the regime which is now in Formosa after being driven off the mainland. The comment I would make there is that if these words mean what they would appear to mean, then we are not prepared to consider agreement on our part to abandon Formosa while communist China is guilty of aggression, but the words mean nothing unless the understanding to be taken from them is that if aggression should stop then our position with regard to Formosa would change. The other point is that we have decided we will do nothing to assist the Chiang forces on Formosa with respect to any action they may take against the mainland.
I submit these are all positive declarations of policy which should be placed before the house before they are stated anywhere else, and that approval should be sought from the House of Commons and the parliament of Canada of statements of policy which may affect the whole future of this country. This is not only the life of Canada. It is the life of this parliament. Unless we are to have authority over decisions affecting the future of Canada, then parliament certainly can no longer claim to assert its proper authority on behalf of the people of Canada.
I am raising this question of privilege as one affecting every member. I most earnestly hope, in view of the speech made in New York on Friday, that, no matter how much any one of us may agree with the views put forward, the Prime Minister will recall the suggestion made a few days ago and will announce now that there will be a debate on external affairs on a motion to approve proposals made by the government, and that on that occasion proposals will be put forward that will indicate what we have undertaken, subject to qualifications, at Lisbon, and also any other proposals such as these so that they may receive the approval or otherwise of this house. If that were done then, as I indicated before, we would not be called upon to carry forward casually, within the broad ambit of the speech from the throne, a debate which should be centred around a clear statement of policy by the government which seeks the approval of the house for that policy.

Mr. Speakers Order. Before the Prime Minister replies, I might say that I think the remarks that have been made by the leader of the opposition show clearly that the rules should be adhered to. I am not criticizing the leader of the opposition for doing it, because, as I said, I allowed it to be done during the last session. He has made a statement with respect to a speech delivered by a minister of the crown outside of this house. Tonight another minister may make another speech. Tomorrow someone else may take exception to it, rise in his place and make a speech with regard to it. The leader of the opposition has stated his views very briefly on certain portions of what was said, and has intimated how he feels about them. Now I see the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar seeking to rise in his place and comment on the speech. I do not know if he does want to comment on it, but I know he was rising in his place to say something before the Prime Minister rose. Having allowed the leader of the opposition to comment, I do not see how I can prevent the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar from doing so, and I do not see how I can prevent other hon. members from doing so. It occurs to me that this question could be raised during the debate on the speech from the throne, and that what has been requested of the government today could be requested in that debate. I merely point that out in order to emphasize that I think we shall make more progress if we abide by the established rules instead of departing from them.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PRO- TEST AGAINST TREATMENT OF CANADIAN NUNS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or, in his absence, to his parliamentary assistant. I have sent notice of my question. What action does the government plan to take in protest against the shocking treatment of five Canadian nuns in Canton recently, and to ensure that Canadian missionaries are protected against such outrages in future?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Lesage (Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRO- TEST AGAINST TREATMENT OF CANADIAN NUNS
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of his question. I believe

little can be added to the statements made in this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on December 3, 1951, and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on December 29, 1951.
However, I am authorized to repeat that the government deplores the shocking treatment the Canadian missionaries in China have received, and has taken every course open to it to protest to the central people's government of the people's republic of China. In the absence of direct Canadian representation in China we have had the assistance not only of the United Kingdom charge d'affaires but of representatives of other countries. On a number of occasions these gentlemen have made strong representations, and there are some signs that in a certain measure they have succeeded in improving the conditions of some imprisoned persons.
The house will no doubt be aware that three of the nuns who were tried in Canton have now reached Hong Kong, and missionaries of all denominations continue to arrive at that place. Whereas on January 1, 1951 there were about 400 Canadians in China, there are now approximately 160, the majority of whom are missionaries; and many of these have applied for exit permits.
The situation, of course, is one of great delicacy; and, as has been pointed out in the past both by the Prime Minister and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the best advice at the disposal of the government indicates that little is to be gained and much may be lost by heated public discussion of those questions. I know the government shares to the full the natural indignation engendered by these events, but it is compelled to suggest, as it has suggested, that the safety of Canadian citizens still in China dictates the utmost caution.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was kind enough to send me notice of this question, and, subject to your ruling, I should be glad to try to answer him.

Mortgage lending has been primarily a field for private investment and one in which the lending institutions have played a leading role. During the past year, however, changes in the money market made mortgages through the National Housing Act less attractive to lending institutions than they were formerly. Accordingly, last June, parliament amended the National Housing Act to encourage lending institutions to continue to lend under its provisions by increasing the rate of interest. In October, increases in the amount of the loan and corresponding reductions in down payments were announced, and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at the same time was authorized to extend greater guarantees to the lending institutions.
These steps have helped to keep mortgage money flowing, and, despite the many problems which must be recognized, I hope that the lending institutions will continue to play their traditional role in this field. In the meantime, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, under section 31A-that is, the section which authorizes Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make direct loans in those fields and areas where the lending institutions do not normally operate -has expanded its operations in a variety of ways, the most important of which are loans for the construction of houses for defence workers, in accordance with the policy announced last October, and loans for rental insurance projects.

subtopic: DEFENCE PREPARATIONS AND FOREIGN POLICY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
subtopic: DEFENCE PREPARATIONS AND FOREIGN POLICY
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister inform us at this time if there is to be a debate on a motion to approve the government's defence preparations and defence production, as one debate, and a separate debate on a motion to approve the government's foreign policy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEFENCE PREPARATIONS AND FOREIGN POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition and I have quite divergent views as to what is the constitutional practice under a monarchical as contrasted with a republican form of government. It has not been the practice, nor is it intended at this session to introduce it as the practice, for the government to come before parliament and ask parliament to approve the responsibility it exercises in advising the Governor General as to administrative government. It has been and will continue to be the practice to declare to the house what the decision of the government is, so that the house, exercising its control over responsible government, may dismiss

the government it dissatisfied with its conduct. That is and always has been the constitutional practice, and so long as I have control over what originates from this side of the house it will continue to be the constitutional practice.
With respect to the question whether there will be one or two or more debates, or whether they will be incorporated into the debate on the address, I had thought there would be opportunity for matters of that kind to be discussed on the motion which is on the order paper to set up a committee to scrutinize defence expenditure. Defence expenditure is required because of the international situation, or the view we take of the international situation; and it is recommended to parliament. I think it is the responsibility of parliament to see that it is wisely made and that it tends to serve the purpose for which the government asks parliament to make the appropriations.
With respect to external affairs, if any new commitment is to be made or to be recommended by the government it will be declared to the house, and will not become a commitment until the house has had an opportunity of saying whether or not it has confidence in a government that is prepared to make that kind of commitment. There would be an opportunity for that in the debate on the address. The Secretary of State for External Affairs had prepared a speech in the form of a report on what had taken place at Lisbon. He had hoped, up to Thursday, that he would have an opportunity of delivering it. He wished to make it in this house before expressing any views that he may be called upon to express in fulfilling the engagement that he had made to speak to the Canadian Society in New York. He had accepted that engagement because he had to be in Washington on business connected with the department, and thought he could be away the additional day of Friday without causing any inconvenience. Unfortunately, there is many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip. Because of an extremely important situation, the first three days of this week had to be devoted to the consideration of matters other than the speech from the throne, and the minister had to leave before there was an opportunity of making that speech.
The minister, as Mr. Pearson, is also the president of the council which met in Lisbon. When he uses the word "we" in his speech that does not necessarily mean the members of the Canadian government or of the Canadian parliament, or even the Canadian people. It means he is speaking as one of a large group, whether the United Nations or the Atlantic treaty council, and has views
Inquiries of the Ministry as to what will best serve the common purpose of deterring aggression. He is expressing views in that regard. I listened with care to what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) had to say. I had seen the report of the speech and I did not find anything new or startling in it; but that may be a matter of interpretation.
To deal specifically with the question, it would be the desire of the government, on the first occasion when there is a government day, to move this motion to set up a committee on defence expenditures. I have been seeking some other matter upon which a debate on external affairs could be brought about at this time without establishing a precedent which I would not be prepared to take the responsibility of establishing, namely that of asking parliament to approve in advance the line of conduct to be taken by the representatives of Canada at these international meetings. I must confess that I have not been able to find the kind of procedure that would not be a departure from our traditional practices.
This motion to set up a committee on defence expenditures would provide an opportunity at least to discuss matters concerning the defence department, and probably also to discuss the reasons which make those policies of the defence department the kind which the government wishes to recommend to parliament. As soon as the estimates are tabled-and the Minister of Finance declared the other day that they were in the hands of the printer and would be tabled as soon as they arrived from the printer-if that takes place before we get a government day, there could be a motion to refer the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to the standing committee. This would afford an opportunity for such a debate. But I cannot go beyond that at this time. The only motion that is ready at this time which would afford an opportunity for such a debate is the one which is on the order paper.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from reading the
speech from the throne, and from what has happened thus far this session, it appears to me that the government is using this session for the purpose of handing out to the people of Canada as many disappointments as possible. I refer particularly to such questions as health insurance, taxation, and other matters about which I will have something to say if time permits.
I feel that one of the greatest disappointments that this government has ever handed to the people of Canada is its failure, after all these years, to take any action with regard to health insurance. That disappointment is heightened by the fact that the government has not even seen fit to carry out its intention of last June that at this session of parliament a special committee on health insurance would be established.
I know the functions of committees of parliament. There are times when they do good work and when that good work is followed up by good legislation. There are other times, however, when the setting up of a committee is just a delaying action. When, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), the government announced on June 21 last that there would be a special committee at this session, I realized that that meant the delay of at least another year in any legislation respecting health insurance. Nevertheless I welcomed the fact that at least that stage, through which we seem to have to go so long as this government is in power, was at last to be reached; that we would have the committee, and that there would then be some possibility of getting health insurance legislation soon thereafter. Despite the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on June 21, 1951, as recorded at page 4462 of Hansard of that year, to the effect that he hoped we would have such a committee at this session, when on February 29 this year I asked how soon that committee would be set up, he told us that the government had given consideration to the matter but had decided that there would be no committee at this session of parliament.
This, Mr. Speaker, is not a subject which should be dealt with in a light manner, as I feel the government is doing. In fact I feel that the government is just playing politics with this question of health insurance, and that what we can now look forward to is the gesture of a committee on this matter
The Address-Mr. Knowles next year just on the eve of an election so that the Liberal party can again try to fool the people with respect to this important matter.
It is high time that any responsible government in this country realized the importance to the people of Canada of dealing more adequately with the whole question of health. Progress is being made, largely through the efforts of the provinces, aided by the federal health grants, in building up our facilities for health care. But the program will not be complete, indeed it will not really be effective until there is provided a means to enable our people to make use of these facilities so that they may get the care they need-in other words to enable our people to pay for the care of their health on some reasonable or rational basis. It is the cost of medical care which prevents our people from getting it today, and that is what is involved in the demand of the Canadian people for health insurance, namely that something be done about the cost side of the whole question of hospitalization and medical care.
This question is by no means new. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) pointed out the other day that health insurance was included in the platform of the Liberal party in 1919 which, even to slow-moving Liberals, is a long time ago. Then, during the forties the question came up for considerable discussion. Indeed in the early forties committees of the house were set up to deal with the matter. Many documents were placed before us, including a draft bill which came before us toward the end of the session of 1943. In 1945 the government made proposals for a national health program, including health insurance as one of the most important aspects of that program.
Hon. members who were here will recall how some of us insisted during the sessions immediately following the making of those 1945 proposals that something should be done without delay about the whole question of health insurance. And it was I feel because of that pressure that Mr. King on May 14, 1948, made the announcement he did make with respect to the federal health grants program now in effect. I well remember that announcement, and I read it again only today. All through the statement he made on that occasion runs the theme that the program then being announced was the taking of the first step toward a program of nation-wide health insurance. Mr. King reviewed the promises that had been made in former years. He reviewed the declared aim of his government and of the Liberal party, and laid emphasis upon the concept of health insurance. He said that that was the purpose

The Address-Mr. Knowles
of the program then being announced, namely that a foundation might be laid for a nationwide program of health insurance.
In subsequent years, those of us in this corner of the house in particular have called upon the government to take the next step, the step that was promised so many years ago. Thus far however that step has not been taken. Finally in June of last year, after three days' debate on the floor of the house, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), as reported at page 4462 of Hansard for June 21, 1951, said-and I quote him exactly-
We will examine that problem, and in the regular session of 1952 I hope that we may be able-and I think I may go further than that and say that we are giving consideration to the matter [DOT]-to set up a parliamentary committee to examine this whole problem.
There follows my word of approval, and the speeches of other hon. members who took part in the debate that day indicated that they accepted the minister's announcement at its face value, and welcomed this expression of hope on the part of the minister that we would have the committee at this session of parliament.
On February 29 of this year, I asked the minister when the committee was going to be set up. In reply he referred back to the statement of last June and said it was really only a promise that the government would consider the matter, and that having considered the matter it had decided that no committee would be set up at this session.
As I read closely the minister's statement of June 21 last I discover that he really said two things. He said that he, personally, hoped we would have a committee at this session. His other statement-given parenthetically- was that the government was giving consideration to the matter. What I would like to know is this: Who in the government has frustrated the minister's hope? Who said no?
I find that hope expressed not only in what the minister said on that occasion, but in the most recent report of the Department of National Health and Welfare, which was laid on the table only a few days ago. True, that report is for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951, nearly a year ago; but we know that these reports are prepared after the end of the fiscal year and, in so far as they contain comments, they reflect current thinking as well as a statement of what happened during that fiscal year.
On looking through the report, I have been interested to find that there are actually more references in it to health insurance than there have been in recent reports of the Department of National Health and

Welfare. While those references do not go quite as far as I would like them to go, they do suggest that the department has been giving considerable thought to the matter. The references suggest to me that the people in the department thought the committee promised last June was going to be established at this session. I find that a statement at page 22 of the report confirms what I said earlier about the national health program, when it says:
The national health program, under which annual federal grants are made to the provinces to strengthen and extend health and hospital services and to lay the foundations for health insurance-
And so on. The point of that quotation is that the department recognizes that the purpose of the present health program is to lay a foundation for national health insurance. Then I turn to pages 61 and 62 of this same report and, under the heading "Health Care Studies," I find a lengthy subsection which reads in part as follows:
Departmental activities in health insurance work are the responsibility of the directorate of health insurance studies, with research studies being conducted by the research division.
During the year a complete re-evaluation of the 1945 proposals for health insurance has been undertaken, with close attention being paid to analysis of systems in operation in all countries, including detailed study of program, administrative methods employed, the success with which objectives are being met, the principal difficulties that have been encountered and costs and methods of financing.
As one goes down through the various paragraphs of this section it is clear that a major interest, a major concern in the Department of National Health and Welfare, has been the study of the question of health insurance, to an extent much greater than has obtained for several years. By reading these excerpts from the report I am led to believe that the people in the department took the minister's statement of last June at its face value, and thought that at this session a special committee would be set up to study the matter.
Then, similarly, at page 102 of the report under the heading "Research Division," which deals with the work of that division, I find that during the year it is said that, among other things, that division worked on the whole question of health insurance.
There you have it. There is a promise dating from 1919, a promise brought to life and renewed during the forties, a promise stated to the house clearly by Mr. King on May 14, 1948, a promise to which references were made frequently during the election campaign of 1949, a promise which, in the light of the statement on June 21 last year by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, we dared to believe was at last on the

way to fulfilment. But come this session, and the answer is that nothing is to be done. I cannot condemn such inaction too strongly.
I realize that last year the general impression was abroad that there might be an election in 1952, and the setting up of a committee on the eve of an election would not have been inconsistent with the way in which this government operates. The general impression now is that the election has been put off until 1953, and so it appears that, similarly, the study of health insurance has been put off.
I wish to condemn as strongly as I can this method of playing politics with a matter of such great importance to the people of this country. I commend all those who have taken part in the progress that has been made in increasing our hospital accommodation, and improving our facilities for medical care. But I say again that not until we have an over-all program that includes health insurance, that provides the means to enable people to pay for the health care that they need, will we have the kind of program we should have, will we have the kind of program that this government has been promising across the years. This is a most urgent matter. I hope we will get action on it soon.
In my opening remarks I suggested that another of the fields in which this government seems to be trying to hand out disappointments to the Canadian people at this session is the field of taxation. This is something that was not referred to in the speech from the throne, but we have had a statement on the matter by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and also a statement, even though somewhat oblique, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It seems clear from those two statements that there will be no significant reductions in taxation at this session of parliament, despite the huge surplus which the Minister of Finance has piled up during this fiscal year.
All of us in this house recognize the need for raising money to meet the services which this house wants to provide for the Canadian people; all of us recognize the tremendous burden of our defence expenditures; but there is still room for adjusting our tax burden on the basis of equity. Furthermore, when there are thess huge surpluses surely now is the time to bring in at least some tax reductions.
What some of us deplore about this whole matter, if I may say so again, is the way in which the government plays politics with this important question.

speechtext: I was just going to deal with the years leading up to 1949. In the years prior to 1949 the government proclaimed and adhered to the theory of cyclical budgeting. I am sure hon. members remember that, although we never hear the phrase used any more. That was proposed with a view to making reductions in the national debt. So there were no significant reductions in taxation. But it appeared to us and it appeared to the people of Canada that what the government was doing during those years was to build up a sufficient surplus so that in an election year they could do both things, they could boast of making a payment against the national debt and at the same time hand out significant tax reductions to try to encourage the people to vote that party back into power.

Does the hon. member for Spadina mean that it was bad to vote that party back into power? To ask the question is but to answer that it certainly was. The people of Canada know it and they have not forgotten the fact that, despite the huge majority the government has here, their majority at the polls was a fraction under 50 per cent of those who voted in June, 1949.
What happened after 1949? We got back into theoretical budgeting, the kind of budgeting that lays a basis for increasing taxation and the building up of surpluses. As years come and go the minister boasts of the fact that he has these surpluses which are much greater than he anticipated. He now says it is a good thing he has them because they can be used to pay off a portion of the national debt. I do not blame the government for trying to underwrite practice with theory, but there is such a thing as consistency. Everyone in this house knows that the minute it is decided

The Address-Mr. Knowles to go to the country these theories will be forgotten and these huge surpluses will be used for the purpose of making tax reductions.

speechtext: Is it not true that in 1950 when we set up the committee on old age security the hon. member said that we had ample information on all these social security measures without setting up further committees?

speechtext: I am not proposing the setting up of a committee to deal with the question of taxation. However, I was deploring the fact that so far as health insurance is concerned the government was not prepared to go even that far. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend. A committee is not needed. The government has abundant material on the whole question of health insurance. But the government wants to do it that way, it wants to proceed in the delaying manner of appointing a committee. And now it is not even prepared to do that.
To get back to this question of taxation. What annoys the Canadian people, what annoys us as their representatives in this parliament, even more than the government's failure to make the necessary taxation adjustments, even more than the failure to make reductions at a time when we have this huge surplus, is the feeling that the government is simply using the taxpayers' money to play with in a political fashion, to try to build up surpluses so that they can be used to reduce taxes-in other words as political bait-in an election year. I deplore that and I suggest as strongly as I can that it does not give strength to democracy in times like these when democracy needs all the strength it can possibly muster.
Another subject in connection with which this government is handing out a disappointment, by its silence, is its failure at this


session, and I say this advisedly despite the thoughts that I know will be in some hon. members' minds, to do anything toward increasing the amount of old age pensions, either under the Old Age Security Act or the Old Age Assistance Act. I know that there are many hon. members who will say that these acts were placed on the statute books only last year and they should be allowed to rest for a while. The trouble is that far too many people in this country find that they simply cannot get by on $40 per month, and we have no right to let the matter rest until that amount is increased.
As I pointed out when these two measures were going through parliament last year, the one during the first session and the other during the second session, the rise in the cost of living since the committee on old age security made its recommendations, the rise in the cost of living since the figure of $40 was arrived at just before the election of 1949, makes it imperative that payments under our old age security measures should be not less than $60 per month. I call upon the government to face up to its responsibility. We have heard talks today about responsible government. All right, the government should consider its responsibility to the people of Canada and I call upon it to face up to its responsibility in this field and bring in a measure increasing the amount of the old age pension paid under these two acts.
As I pointed out last fall, to increase the amount paid under the Old Age Security Act from $40 to $60 per month would cost only another $160 million a year. That is a lot of money to any of us as individuals, but it is a small amount of money in terms of the kind of budgets that we have at the present time. Similarly, to increase the amount paid under the Old Age Assistance Act would take a relatively small amount of money compared to what it would mean to those people who are affected, and compared to what it would mean in terms of strengthening democracy, strengthening what is sometimes referred to as "our way of life". I press that demand as strongly as I can, and all hon. members know that I will continue to do so until we get action.
Speaking of old age pensions, it has been a matter of great disappointment to many people to discover that the position has not yet been made clear with respect to recoveries from the estates of persons who were on the former old age pension up to December 31, 1951. I raised this question in the house on June 23, 1951, as can be

found by referring to pages 4586 and 4587 of Hansard for that date. On that occasion I had this to say:
I hope the minister will not say that this matter has to wait until the fall, because it is a matter that is of concern to many pensioners right now. What will be the situation with respect to liens on the property of persons now 70 and over?
The minister and I got into a bit of a crossfire based mainly on confusion as to my use of the word "liens". We eventually got that straightened out, and it was clear then and it is clear now that liens under that former act were placed not by Ottawa but by the provincial governments. But they were placed there because the federal act had in it a clause which said that the provinces had to agree to make recoveries from the estates of deceased pensioners. In other words, the provinces used liens to enable them to carry out the federal government's demand for recoveries. When we finally got that bit of confusion straightened out, I put the matter to the minister in these direct words, speaking of these people who were on the former old age pension:
Will they be treated exactly the same as people who will go on the new universal pension starting in January?
The minister's reply was:
That is a matter that will have to be decided in the future. I cannot decide it now.
What has happened since then is that several of the provinces, accepting the spirit of the new legislation and being anxious to do the fair thing, have passed statutes cancelling all liens against the property of persons who received pensions under the former Old Age Pensions Act. But they have discovered that, although they have the right to cancel those liens, they cannot stop seeking to make recoveries out of the estates of these persons after they pass on. The reason they have to continue making these parliament despite the huge surplus which liens is because the federal government has refused to make any change in the agreements with the provinces, or to make any change in the regulations or in the legislation under which those agreements were drawn.
I remind hon. members that in 1943 Mr. Ilsley, who as minister of finance was in charge of old age pensions at that time, met our request part way and wrote to the provinces and told them that the making of recoveries could henceforth be limited to estates in excess of $2,000. If the government then had the power-under the act, under the regulations and under the agreements that had been made-to draw a line and say that recoveries only had to be made in the case of estates in excess of $2,000,
I submit that the federal government has
The Address-Mr. Knowles the power now to say to the provinces: You need not make any more recoveries whatsoever out of the estates of persons who were drawing pension prior to December 31, 1951. Several provinces, as I say, have come up against this situation. I know they have in Saskatchewan and Manitoba as well as in others. I have in my hand a copy of the Votes and Proceedings of the legislative assembly of Manitoba for February 12, 1952. It records a lengthy statement on this matter by the Hon. Ivan Schultz, minister of health and welfare for that province. He says in part:
In regard to the collection of claims against the estates of deceased pensioners in this group-
He is referring to those who drew pensions prior to this year under the old Old Age Pensions Act.
-the legislation of the federal government and the obligations under the agreement submitted for signature by the federal government compel this province, in accordance with similar agreements with every other province, to collect from the estates of deceased pensioners where the estate is over $2,000 net. Neither Manitoba nor any other province has any option in this matter at the present time.
Last June the Minister of National Health and Welfare played around with this question and said that liens were a provincial matter. All right. Provinces like Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and perhaps others-I know about the three I have mentioned because I have seen the legislation- have cancelled their liens. Yet they find that even though they have cancelled these liens they are still required under the terms of the federal agreement to seek to make recoveries out of estates for pensions paid prior to December 31, 1951.
I submit this is completely out of keeping with the recommendations of the committee on old age security. It is completely out of keeping with the whole debate that took place in the house last June and again in October and November. I call upon the government to take action similar to that taken by Mr. Ilsley in 1943 and to make it clear to the provinces that henceforth, indeed as from January 1, 1952, they need make no further recoveries whatsoever from the estates of deceased pensioners.
I turn now to another question. Here too, although there has been an announcement in the speech from the throne that something will be done, I fear we may be in for disappointment. I refer to the proposal to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, something that we asked for with all the power at our command during the fall session of 1951. I suppose there are members on the government side who will say to me: Why do

The Address-Mr. Knowles you not wait and see what is in that legislation? I should like to oblige them but it so happens I have seen press reports as to what that legislation is likely to include. I know that press reports can be wrong but these friends of ours in the press gallery often have an uncanny way of finding out what is going to be included in anticipated legislation.
The reports I have seen suggest that it is the government's intention to raise the war veterans allowance to $50 for a single veteran and $85 for a>
married veteran. That will be a bitter disappointment. When the Canadian Legion asked for a minimum of $50 single and $100 married I think they were being most conservative, reasonable and responsible. I think they should have asked for more. I think they should have asked for not less than $60 single and $120 married. But in the light of what they asked for, if the government only gives $85 for a married pensioner on the burnt-out pension it will be a bitter blow and disappointment for which the government must be severely condemned.
I hope by suggesting this condemnation in advance they will change their minds with respect to that matter.
Another aspect of the rumoured legislation on war veterans allowance is that the income ceilings will be increased slightly so as to permit burnt-out pensioners who are drawing old age security payments to get a little more of the burnt-out pension than they are now receiving. A very common example at the present time is that of a single burnt-out pensioner who was (formerly getting $40.41 by way of burnt-out pension. Many of these men who are over 70 have qualified for the $40 old age security payment. There is no means test under the Old Age Security Act but it is still there in the War Veterans Allowance Act with the result that their war veterans allowance has been reduced from $40.41 right down to $10.83. Thus they are now receiving $40 in old age security and $10.83 as a war veterans allowance, making a total between the two pensions of $50.83. Clearly what is called for is not just a slight increase in the amount of other income allowed under the War Veterans Allowance Act but the complete removal of the means test so far as the war veterans allowance is concerned.
I have been amazed and pleased at the large number of people who have spoken to me about this matter in the last few months, particularly non-veterans, who have said to me time and again that surely this burnt-out pension is something that should be paid without the means test. I know the means test is gone from the Old Age Security Act; but it is very hard to explain to the pensioner,

who has his burnt-out pension reduced when he gets his old age security pension, that the means test is gone. As far as he is concerned it may be gone from one act but it is not gone from the other, so he is still under a means test. I insist, Mr. Speaker, that this is one disappointment which this government must not continue to perpetrate upon the people of this country; that is, niggardly treatment of our burnt-out pensioners. I suggest that the government should go the whole way when that legislation is brought in.
At the same time I feel that something should be done with regard to section 33 of the Pension Act. I regret there is no reference to that in the speech from the throne. Under section 33 of the Pension Act what are known as compassionate pensions are paid, such as pensions to dependent parents, dependent widowed mothers and so on. Section 33 is in the Pension Act, but it is still under a means test. When we were discussing this matter at the fall session I made a plea to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) to remove the means test from section 33. He contended that this was not really necessary, for after all the members of the pension commission were anxious to do their best by those affected by this section. On November 30, 1951, as reported at page 1490 of Hansard, the minister said:
That is not what happened when the last increase took place. At that time these cases were reviewed by the commission, and a great majority of them were increased because the decision of the commission was taken in the light of the general increases that had1 been given. I have every reason to believe that that will be the way the commission will review these cases. My horn, friend of course realizes that decisions or actions taken by the commission are not at the discretion of the minister, but I think that past experience would show that we can fairly well rely on a generous attitude on their part.
Well, I dared, to hope that that might be the result, and! no doubt it has been in some cases. They would be the cases we do not hear about. But a number of cases have already been drawn to my attention of dependent parents now receiving the old age security pension and having their dependents pension either reduced or cut off altogether. A case was drawn to any attention just a few days ago of dependent parents, where the father formerly had a C.P.B. pension of $36 a month and the mother a dependent parents' pension of $30 a month, and one other contribution of $10 a month. The father is now over 70, so he gets the $40 old age security pension; but the mother's $30 dependent's pension has been discontinued altogether. That is not carrying out the spirit of what the minister said to me on November 30, 1951; and I am more convinced now than I was then that

the only way to deal properly with section 33 of the Pension Act is to remove the means test from it altogether, and to increase the amounts paid under that section.
Another case I would mention is that of a lady 81 years of age who is in an institution for older people in the province of Manitoba. For some 16 years she has been receiving $50 a month under section 33 of the Pension Act. The institution where she is being cared for has taken $45 a month, leaving her $5 for necessities and personal expenditures. What has happened to her? She now gets the $40 old age security pension so the $50 under section 33 of the Pension Act has been reduced, by the commission to $35. Thus she now gets a total of $75 a month; but the institution takes $70, so she is left with the same $5 she had before. That is not good1 enough.
There are scores of cases of this kind, which suggest that so long as the means test is retained in the War Veterans Allowance Act and so long as it is retained in section 33 of the Pension Act, we are going to have a great many people in this country feeling that even with the means test removed from the Old Age Security Act, it has not been removed so far as they are concerned. I call upon the government to take action on this question, not piecemeal, not in a niggardly fashion, but on an over-all basis at this session of parliament.
I see that my time is running along, and I am going to have to compress into a sentence or two each a good many subjects with which I was going to deal. I said at the outset that this is a session of disappointments which the government is handing out to the Canadian people. Another of those is with respect to superannuated civil servants. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) made reference to them the other night; but in his praise of the speech from the throne he did not seem to realize that there is no reference in that speech to anything being done for them. I feel the same about the attitude of the government toward retired pensioners of the Canadian National Railways. It is fine for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to boast of improvements that are being made

The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell things which unite us are greater than the things which divide us. This pleasant custom is one of the things that remind us of that fact.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to make some remarks about foreign trade, and then some remarks about the subject which has already been discussed a great deal, namely the inflationary prices and the effect on them of taxation and of the large surplus. It seems, perhaps, a suitable time to be discussing foreign trade because tomorrow the chancellor of the British exchequer is to present his first budget in circumstances which are grave to the point of the greatest anxiety. Often we talk as if we were immune from all these worries. I shall have something to say about that in a moment or two.
First, I want to recall to members that a tremendous change has taken place in the course of trade within the last few years. Last year exports to the United States amounted to $2,297 million approximately, and to the United Kingdom, $631 million, a great deal less than a third as much. It is not so many years since the figures were relatively equal, and without wearying you with a lot of details I register that one figure because I think it is a matter upon which we should reflect.
It is the duty of reasonable men to try to look forward and consider the consequences of their own actions. I propose to make some comments on this trade situation. The British chancellor's speech tomorrow is coupled in one's mind with the difficulties which have suddenly overtaken Australia. I do not know why it should be sudden, but at any rate the Australians are busy trying to take steps to curtail imports, just as the British are doing.
What does this mean to us? Sometimes I think, with all due deference to them, that the government has been riding on the crest of a boom for so long that they may fall into the great error of thinking that booms go on forever. Sometimes I recall the old cliche of Dr. Coue who said: "Every day in every way we are getting better and better." I sometimes wonder whether it is not difficult for the government to take these things as seriously as they might. There are many interests in this country who take the present trade situation very seriously. The cheese producers, for one, have been entirely cut off from the British market. The apple growers in British Columbia and the maritime provinces will be extremely anxious, as will the grain farmers and indeed people right across the dominion. It may be said that in particular the provinces east and

west will suffer, but of course we in the central provinces will suffer too, though not quite so acutely.
I ask the question again: To what extent are we perturbed by this situation as I feel we should be? There is an old music hall ditty, which some of you will remember, which says that "where there is a will there are three ways." On the other hand, if there is no will there is not even one way. Sometimes as I read the press, and as I read those dispatches which we all feel are pleasantly inspired from authoritative quarters, I feel that we think of ourselves as lifted up above all the worries that affect the lesser breeds without the law-those unfortunate people that are up against difficulties at the moment.
Recently the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) went to London to attend the commonwealth conference. I am sure he was welcome there. A Canadian Press dispatch appeared on January 12 commenting on Mr. Abbott's departure. I am quite sure that this attitude did not come from the minister but this is what the report says:
Finance Minister Abbott will leave tor London to lend a sympathetic ear to Britain's financial troubles.
I have no doubt the minister did that, and did it in a sympathetic manner. The report continues:
Officials say that Canada, as a dollar country, feels she is on the sidelines in the current crisis, and she is affected only indirectly.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, that came from a source which one usually believes has access to those speakers who are never mentioned by name, but who seem to speak with considerable knowledge. What I should like to ask is whether the man who wrote that dispatch or the people who inspired that dispatch really are taking seriously enough the fact that Britain is our second best customer? In fact, she is the first best customer to a great many people in this country. If that market, which is already seriously damaged, were to be damaged still further the consequences, to put it mildly, would be serious-indeed, far more than serious; they could be absolutely vital to us.
Last autumn the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) used reassuring words. He said we were doing our best to explore other markets, and I am sure he meant that. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) seemed to have a certain amount of worry, because it is reported in the Canadian press: . . . that Finance Minister Abbott said production ought to be up. I told him it might be a good thing if you were to go over to Britain to see if financing could be arranged so that production couldi be up.

I seem to remember that a few years ago the Minister of Agriculture was very impatient at the financial barriers in the way of trade and thought they ought to be swept away. It is not quite so easy as that. According to the report the minister goes on to say:
From reports coming back I rather think that he-
That is the Minister of Finance.
-has been able to do something along that line.
A day or two later the Canadian Press from London reported Mr. Abbott as saying that the commonwealth discussions did not include detailed talks on Anglo-Canadian trade, and it seemed "unrealistic" at this time to expect an increase in United Kingdom purchases. We all understand what was in the mind of the minister when he said that, but I come back to the fact that if we accept that position, if we really believe that is the situation and we cannot do anything about it, then we will not do anything about it. I noticed that last December the Winnipeg Free Press said that we were enjoying an abundant foreign market for our exports which were at an all-time peak. Well, that is very comforting. If we let it go at that we might travel along without worry, but I suggest that we have had an indication in the last few days, with the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, how quickly the United States can act when they are alarmed. I suggest that when we are flattering ourselves and taking comfort from this very large trade with the United States, we should never forget that the United States is highly competitive with us in many ways; that those large exports are to a large extent the result of the boom; that when the United States feels its interests are affected it can be rather ruthless in shutting out foreign goods.
Going back a few years, we all remember the Hawley-Smoot and Fordney-McCumber tariffs. We have already evidence that congress is cramping the style of the United States administration and seeking to prevent them from giving full effect to some of the agreements which we thought were in full effect. I say, therefore, however true in a technical way it may be to say that Canada is on the sidelines, I think it is highly unrealistic if we have not got in mind that the recovery of the British market is something to which we should be giving the closest thought.
As I said a moment ago, when we recall how much of our economy is dependent on the British market, we need only allow our minds to consider-and it is not a thing that one even wants to mention, but over there the ugly word "bankruptcy" has been used; Churchill has used it-"'hat could happen if
The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell we were really cut off from the British market, and what it would mean to our prairie provinces, to the maritimes and to British Columbia in particular. I therefore say that it ought to be one of the strongest preoccupations in our minds to do everything we possibly can and to make every effort to get back this market. The exchange between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) does not entirely reassure us. It stresses the difference of opinion that exists.

The minister referred to government as a business. Well, government is not a business. The oft-quoted words of Philip Snowden will show that. I think the taxpayer will find it much harder to accept the statement that taxes may not be reduced in view of the fact that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have both expressed, not only no dissatisfaction and no regret that the level of taxation produced $700 million surplus this year; they have both approved it and suggested that it is a good thing. Mr. Speaker, my first word must be one of thanks to my deskmate, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), for making way for me this afternoon. When I came into the house I had no desire


or intention of speaking in this debate, but when I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) expand the wide field which he generally covers in debates in the house to include for the first time the Department of Finance I felt that he deserved an immediate reply. Any hon. member is interested when another hon. member indicates interest in his riding, and any minister or parliamentary assistant is naturally gratified when hon. members express interest in their sphere of operation. The opening point I should like to make is that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had better devote a lot more interest to the Department of Finance and taxation policy before he goes into a full forty-minute speech on that department. I recall, for example, that he mentioned the fact we had this policy of cyclical budgeting, of taxing stiffly in good years to pay off debt, the old biblical injunction, the policy followed by any good farmer, fisherman, or housewife of paying off your debts in good days so you will be in good shape if rainy days should come. Then he went on to say that this policy was immediately abandoned in election years and just used in off-election years. I am afraid he is not as careful a student of the public accounts as of other public documents because at pages 110 and 111 of the public accounts a record is given of the debt reduction of all governments since 1867.
In particular in the post-war years since 1945 it shows that there has been a substantial debt reduction in every year, not just off-election years. In 1949 there was a debt reduction of over $500 million, and in 1950 a debt reduction of $131 million. It is quite true that in the spring of 1949, because of the expanding economy and because of the fact that civilian goods were again coming on the market in adequate supply, there were tax reductions, but there were also tax reductions in the fall budget of 1949, and there were also tax reductions in the spring budget of 1950. In 1950, however, occurred an event which apparently very conveniently slips the hon. member's mind at times. In June of 1950 came aggression in Korea, and that more than anything else changed this trend of taxation reductions, a trend which was still piling up surpluses however because the expanding economy was able to allow for gradual tax reduction and still accumulate surpluses for debt reduction.
We tried to remind the Canadian people of the impact of Korea on our taxation system by specifically putting the defence surcharge on top of the previous rates of corporation

tax and personal income tax. That is a constant reminder, and that is the reason for the reversal of this trend of tax reduction, not just of having surpluses and applying them to debt reduction, but being able to reduce taxation as the economy and trade have expanded. However, I would also recall that the hon. member also advocated tax reduction. In this connection his views are a little different from those in a document I was reading, while he was speaking, on the financial problems of the United Kingdom. I note that the trade union congress of Great Britain, which is affiliated with the Labour party, is actually recommending an increase of 6 pence in the pound on income taxation to meet the present emergent situation because of Korea, and they are also strongly advocating that the government should budget for a healthy surplus, as we do in this country.
However, in the end the member finished his little dissertation on taxation and then turned to the main body of his speech which I can sum up by saying that he was advocating bigger and bigger expenditures out of the public treasury. If he can come forward in a later full-dress speech on finance and tell us how to accomplish this age-old miracle always promised by oppositions, of lower taxes and increased expenditures, I am sure every member in the house will listen to him very closely. The easiest way in the world for a minister of finance to seek cheap popularity is by cutting taxes, racking up expenditures and then leaving the mess to his successor, but the difference in the case of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) of course is that his successor, no matter when he retires, will be a Liberal minister of finance, and the successor to the present government will be a Liberal government. Therefore we are going to keep our house in order for this long-range objective, and not court the easy popularity which is won for a year or two by such a program of tax cutting and overexpenditures.
I am particularly delighted to see the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in the house because while I am on my feet I intend to comment briefly on the remarks he made on taxes in his speech of March 6. The leader of the opposition has many admirable qualities, but I think one quality he has not got is a sense of humour. I want to point this out to you by reading an excerpt from the bottom of page 159 of Hansard of that date. He had this to say:
Some of the finest examples of parliamentary oratory and democracy are to be found in speeches made by those who have spoken from conviction against a government formed from the party to

I am particularly pleased that in speaking at this time I should have the opportunity of following the financial critic of the opposition. I recognized that he was using some of the notes he had not used during our joint debate on the C.B.C. not very long ago so I sent to my office to get some of the notes I too had not used at that time. I think we can carry on quite nicely from there. First of all he said today that we did not realize we were riding on the crest of a boom and that we should pay more attention to his wise advice. I have got two pages of his wise advice here which I have collected from old Hansards. Every year as financial critic he has stood in his place and predicted gloom.

The Address-Mr. Sinclair If it was not the collapse of the British market it was difficulties with United States exchange. Everything was going wrong. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was a super-optimist because in the post-war years he predicted expanding employment, expanding income and expanding trade for Canada. I have several quotations here. For example, in 1946 this was his wise advice to the Minister of Finance, as found at page 3214 of Hansard:
. . . notwithstanding his rather optimistic forecast it seems to me it is doubtful whether he is going to get the production that he wished.
At page 3217 he predicted dwindling trade and growing unemployment, and came out very strongly at that time against deficit financing. That year we finished with a record surplus, record trade and record employment, so that his wise advice was not very wise at the time. It is wise now of course with hindsight. At page 3217 he said he found "the minister's picture tinged with a certain unreality". Then again next year, in 1947, as found at page 2800 of Hansard, he was again full of gloom. He had this to say:
. . . this situation which the minister shows us is not anything like as good as those figures would indicate.
That was his forecast of a surplus.
In fact it is a very dangerous situation.
However, once again of course the surplus did exceed the very cautious estimate made by the Minister of Finance. Very interestingly, at page 2802 of Hansard for the same year he came out very strongly for a policy of debt reduction by paying off maturing loans out of current government resources which we have been doing. In 1950, however, he was again giving wise advice to the minister. The minister had predicted a $20 million surplus. The financial critic derided him for this and at page 1525 of Hansard for that year he had this to say:
I have tried to show the house that the situation is clear, that the best we can do, even if things are good in the coming year, is to break even.
Things were good that year and we did more than break even. Once again we racked up a good surplus in place of the deficit he was so gloomily predicting at the beginning of the year.

Then he gets along to this matter of forecasting. Perhaps I should return to the leader of the opposition as far as forecasting is concerned. In his speech, to which I have referred, the hon. gentleman calls the minister's forecast in regard to the last budget the worst miscalculation in Canadian history. Well, a budget forecast in a country like Canada is a very difficult thing. The Minister of Finance has to steer a middle course between the gloom and pessimism of the opposition and the optimism of those on this side, who recognize that the government of this country is in good hands and that the Canadian people are going ahead. The minister has to be cautious, for with a steeply graduated income tax such as we have and a heavy corporation tax, the actual revenues are extremely subject to fluctuation if there should be a falling off of trade, which hon. gentlemen opposite have been forecasting in recent years.
However, in connection with this question, since the leader of the opposition said this was the worst forecast in Canadian history,

I thought I would look up some other forecasts of other Canadian ministers in the past. In deference to the Conservative party I turned' first of all to a very great minister of finance, R. B. Bennett. The present Minister of Finance is 8 per cent out in his estimate of revenue, and we are 10 per cent down in our estimate of expenditure, mainly defence expenditure. However, when R. B. Bennett was minister of finance he was always out too. In 1931 he was out not 8 per cent but 17 per cent in his estimate of revenue; and not up, but down. The next year he was exactly the same; he was 17 per cent down, and had a big deficit.
To the south in the United States we have an economy comparable to our own. Last year the secretary of the treasury in the United, States estimated revenue at $37 billion. He actually got over $48 billion. In that year the revenue was up not by 8 per cent but by 29 per cent, as compared with the 8 per cent increase in our revenues. Even better, let us look elsewhere here in Canada, because after all this is our own economy. Let us look at the three provinces which have or had Conservative ministers of finance. The provinces have a much easier time forecasting their revenues because these revenues are more stable: the land taxes, timber and mining royalties, the liquor profits, the gasoline tax, and the federal subsidies. In Ontario Premier Frost is treasurer; and I think everyone in this house irrespective of party politics will agree that Premier Frost is a great improvement over the last premier of Ontario. He estimated a revenue of $228 million, and finished up with $265 million. He was out 16 per cent, as compared to the 8 per cent error in the federal estimates. In Quebec Mr. Gagnon, the provincial treasurer-and those of us who recall the Drew-Duplessis axis recognize, of course, that the Union Nationale is the French-Canadian branch of the Conservative party-estimated revenue of $201 million. He finished' up with $238 million. He was out 18J per cent, as against the federal error of 8 per cent. Out in British Columbia Mr. Anscomb, the Conservative who has since been fired though not for his error in forecasting, was out 17J per cent in his estimate of revenue, again a surplus.
The extraordinary thing by the standards of both the leader of the opposition and the financial critic, however, is that these three provincial Conservative finance ministers are not at all sorry about their surpluses; they are very proud of them. They will use them at election time to indicate the sound position in which their provincial finances were, even though they were much worse calculators
The Address-Mr. Sinclair than the example given by the leader of the opposition as the worst calculation in Canadian history.
Now I go along to the next point made, in connection with this surplus of $722 million for nine months. That is always said with the inflection on the nine months, to give the public the impression that by the end of the year it will be up around a billion dollars. Once again we can look at the record and see the pattern. Our collection of revenues is pretty even right through the year; but in common with all governments, all business and all individuals, the major expenses are in the last quarter of the year. In December of 1949 we had a surplus of roughly $300 million. By the end of March, the end of our fiscal year, not that we had shrunk our money away or wasted it but because we had made the expenditures approved by parliament, that had fallen to $131 million, or less than half. In December of 1950 the surplus was $420 million. By the end of the fiscal year it was down to $211 million. It is true that as of last December the surplus was $722 million. I am not forecasting, but if that pattern is followed the surplus should be down to $400 or $450 million by the end of the year, when the expenditures approved by parliament have been made.	[DOT]
