I figure it out in the very simplest way, by actually looking at the current receipts of revenue against the estimated receipts of revenue. If you will give a little more study to it you will find in the case of the provinces the estimates of revenue were high while the estimates of expenditure were low. They got more and spent more than they estimated, whereas it worked the other way with us. Our expenditures were much lower than we estimated and our revenues were much higher so the gap was opened up in that way. I am glad to be helpful to the hon. member. At the present time we are 8 per cent above in revenue and 10 per cent down in spending.
That raises another point which was brought up by the financial critic. He said of course with that money lying around loose what a temptation it would be to the genial Minister of Public Works to go ahead with public works expenditures. Once again, if hon. members will examine the public works estimates they will find why we in British Columbia, in a very friendly way, call the minister "Revote Fournier". Far from spending up to the limit each year there is substantial underexpenditure. My recollection

The Address-Mr. Sinclair is that this year only two-thirds of what was actually voted for public works has been expended, again because of control by treasury board of such expenditures, not because of anything said by the opposition members, each of whom in turn has been advocating bigger and better expenditures for public works by the government, and of course lower taxes as well.
The next point that is made continually is that this money was taken by the government from the taxpayers, as though the government were highway robbers. To begin with, the government is only the taxpayers of Canada, and the taxpayers are in the position of owing a very large sum of money because of previous expenditures. Our net national debt in 1945 was $13J billion. Since the leader of the opposition is always keen on turning these things into per capita figures, that means every person in this country owes $1,000 as his share of the national debt. To use the example he uses all the time, a family of five is faced with a $5,000 share of the national debt. Well, on that $5,000 share there comes the problem of paying interest at 3 per cent; and the interest on the individual share of the national debt amounts to $30 per person. If you look at the public accounts you will see that figure is pretty accurate, because we pay about $427 million in interest charges on the national debt. So we are faced with this fact, that even with the reductions we have made in our national debt each person in Canada today owes about $1,000 of that debt. We have better times in Canada than we ever had in all our history.
What does a good man do in good times? He pays off his debts, and that is what we are doing for all the nation. The interesting thing is that if the surplus at the end of the year is of the order of $400 million or $500 million, it will be roughly the same as our current interest payment. So far as the government is concerned, the per capita payment of interest of $30 will be matched by a reduction in principal of about $30. I do not think many people with mortgages on their homes, or with business debts, would think they were doing very well if in years as good as this they were only meeting the interest on their debt and not reducing the principal by the amount of the interest; that is all we are doing in Canada today.
However, I should like to mention next this matter of prices. The financial critic raised the point of the prices of electrical appliances, and he used Kate Aitken in a paid advertisement as an authority. It is true that the prices of electrical appliances are up. The wages of the workers are up, and the general income of

those people who sell these appliances is up. The figures furnished by the dominion bureau of statistics and quoted in a very negative fashion by the member for Winnipeg North Centre today show, according to the hon. member, that the average wage does buy a little more goods than in 1939. The point is that it still buys more.
There is one thing I should like to say about the prices of electrical appliances. I believe every member in this house has received copies of advertisements from the Vancouver papers showing substantial reductions in the prices of electrical appliances. There is no thanks due to the Tory party for this, because they fought the abolition of resale price maintenance so vigorously in a filibuster last fall.

I must admit that it is not a happy position to be the financial critic of this government's policies; to have to look back over his speeches to see where he forecast gloom, depression and the collapse of trade, and to realize that he has to stand up and do the same thing next year on equally bad ground. He is in a very difficult position, and so he may be inclined to exaggerate about all this money lying around loose for the government to use. I would be inclined to admit that, being a member supporting the government and the assistant to the Minister of Finance, I may be inclined to view things in too rosy a way. It is for that reason that I am pleased to have this impartial standard set up by the financial critic of the opposition by means of which we may test the budget.

On page 3222 of Hansard for July 8, 1946, the financial critic of the opposition had this to say:
Really the one inescapable test of the minister's budget is this: Does it help to create production? Does it encourage the investor to invest, the producer to produce, the workman to produce his maximum? So far as it does these things it is a success: so far as it does not, it is a failure.
Let us take these things in turn. First, there is production. The hon. member pointed out that this year we had the greatest gross national product in all our history, $21 billion. True, he said that part of that is due to higher prices and so the dollar value is up, but the real value is up 6 per cent. Any country that can increase its real national product by 6 per cent is doing very well, so we pass the first test.

Perhaps the hon. member will permit me to finish my analysis, because he has set us such a good standard; it is so encouraging.
The second test concerns the investor. I think every Canadian knows we have had the greatest per capita capital investment of any country in the world, the greatest in our history. There has been' $4.5 billion in' new capital flowing into new factories, new mines, new transportation, new hydroelectric plants and so on in just the last year.
Only $800 million of that was foreign capital, and the remainder was Canadian., out of our own savings, personal and corporate.
Let us look at the savings of our people. After Korea they did fall to about 1 per cent of disposable personal income because of panic buying. Last year these savings rose to 5 per cent or $700 million, and this year the actual personal savings in Canada of disposable income is a record of 10 per cent or $1,400 million. This was exceeded in only one year in recent years and that was 1943 when we forced people to save through the compulsory savings plan and war bonds and they couldn't spend much money because of rationing.
We have dealt with production so now we come to the test, "the workman to produce his maximum". The financial critic did mention the fact that there has been spotty unemployment this year. He did not mention that, despite all that, on the over-all average, and it is the nation as a whole that must be assessed, in the past year we have had the highest level of employment, the highest level of wages and the best working conditions for Canadian labour in all our history. On the basis, therefore, of these impartial stan-
The Address-Mr. Sinclair dards set two or three years ago by the financial critic when he was again prophesying gloom and disaster, the budgets of the Minister of Finance have been a resounding success. I appreciate, of course, that his present standards are different.
There is one other point about this that I want to mention. Whenever I hear a .criticism of the surplus I think of the very easy task it would be for the financial critic and the leader of the opposition to speak in this debate if, instead of having surpluses, we had deficits, instead of having this excess revenue of 8 per cent because of steadily improving conditions, we had gone down in the hole by $722 million. If that were the case, during the present debate on the speech from the throne you would not be able to keep any of the Tories down, instead of seeing them fold up on their leader's amendment on the first day.
I feel that every member in the house should study these pages 110 and 111 of the public accounts because they show the financing record of all the parties that have been in power since confederation. The summary is here and it shows that in thirty-seven years of Tory rule since 1867 there have been only four years in which a Tory minister of finance managed to have a surplus and so lighten the burden of debt. In those years they managed to reduce the total debt by $28 million- Every other year the Tories were in power they added immeasurably to the public debt. We have been in power for forty-eight years, and in sixteen of those years there were surpluses by means of which we reduced the debt by $2,280 million.
In particular, I would refer members to the record on page 111, the record of this government and especially of this Minister of Finance in debt reduction since the end of the war. We ended the war with a net national debt of around $13.5 billion. Since that time we have, by the courageous policy of taxing for debt reduction in good times, reduced the net debt by $2.5 billion. At the 3 per cent rate that is a saving in interest alone of $75 million a year to all the people of Canada. It is for that reason more than anything else, the sound financial policy of this government, that money has flowed into this country for investment from every country in the world, and which has resulted in the Canadian dollar, out on the open, free markets of the world, being a better dollar than the United States dollar. That is the record, and that is the real test of our financial policies.

I was a year out. I made the suggestion then that, having regard to the plans of the government to alter the basis of representation, the provinces had the right to be consulted. However, that was not the view of the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the prime minister of that time, or indeed of the government. The view taken was that the question of representation was one that affects parliament alone, that it was a federal matter and did not require consultation with or, much less, consent of the provinces. If that is the view of the government now, then this matter could be dealt with through amendment to the constitution in respect of federal matters which now fall within the jurisdiction of parliament.
I am not one who believes that it is a matter for parliament alone. I still adhere to the view that the provinces have a right to be consulted in the matter of determining any change in the basis of representation. For that reason, on behalf of the people on the prairies who are particularly affected at this time, I suggest the calling of a dominion-provincial conference in order to assure
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
agreement that the provinces who will otherwise lose representation shall not have representation reduced to the numbers which would be the result if the ordinary basis of representation is applied.
You ask me what, in general, I suggest. During the dinner recess I tried as clearly as I could to make a summary of the representation I would like to have, and I offer this merely for the purpose of consideration. The prairie provinces have very large constituencies. On the basis of size even now, it is difficult for any member to represent some of the rural constituencies. It will be that much worse if the representation is reduced by one-quarter or, in other words, if there is an increase by one-quarter in the present areas of the constituencies.
The same argument applies in respect of the constituency represented by the hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River (Mr. Simmons). He represents an empire, an area far beyond the possibilities of proper representation by any man. I submit that careful thought should be given to the division of that area in northern Canada into two constituencies.
There is a principle in the constitution now recognized in the maritime provinces that, regardless of population, the representation of the provinces shall not fall below a certain level. Without in any way interfering with the necessary increases that will fall to other provinces in the dominion, by reason of increase in their population, I think it is not unfair to suggest a minimum number of members for each and every province beyond which regardless of population representation would not go.
Without in any way constituting a travesty on the fabric of confederation, this would assure reasonable representation and would deny the injustice that will be done to the prairies if by agreement with the provinces the present system, a system which is manmade and therefore can be man-unmade, is not changed.
I place this before the house not as a considered but rather as a tentative basis. In no way will it deprive any of the provinces of Canada of proper representation; rather it would assure to all ten provinces that in the years ahead their representation in the parliament in Canada shall never fall below a set and fixed level.
I care not what one's party belief may be; there is no division on this question on the prairies. I am sure I am speaking for people outside the house who hold political views different from my own when I say that a reduction in the number of seats in the prairies is a denial of the consideration we

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker have a right to expect. I shall say more when the discussion takes place on second reading of the bill before the house. It is a matter which transcends party considerations. It is one that strikes at the very life of our western provinces and deserves every consideration on the part of the government to assure that in consultation with the provinces-after all, confederation is based upon agreement-some basis will be arrived at which will assure that representation shall not be diminished beyond a certain and fixed limit.
Having said that, I want now to pass on to one or two other matters that are of importance to the prairies. We had a lengthy discussion last week on hoof-and-mouth disease, and I shall refer to that later if I have the time. Another problem that faces us today is the storage and disposal of the damp and tough wheat that we have in such abundance.
First, something will have to be done in order to assure that it will be transported and dried. Something will have to be done now in order to assure the necessary storage facilities. I am not going into particulars, but I have here the Hansard for last fall when week after week I brought up the matter and pointed out the peril facing the western farmer, having regard to the fact that so much of his wheat, barley and oats was damp and so much was under the snow as a result of the inclement weather in the fall. Over and over again the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in semi-optimistic statements promised that there was nothing to worry about. On February 29 I asked him a question and his answer is reported at page 18 of Hansard as follows:
Additional drying capacity is being installed at the head of the lakes, and I believe at Vancouver. Unfortunately time will not permit much help from that source for this year. Arrangements have been made to ship ten million bushels of damp wheat from the prairies to Duluth to take advantage of drying capacity there.
The minister stated that he was hopeful there would be no spoilage, but as I see it that statement is not in accordance with the facts. The situation is assuming tragic proportions. With the approach of spring the prairie provinces are faced with a situation which may result in a loss of from $75 million to $100 million on crops that could be avoided even now provided the government, with its

monopoly power over marketing transport and storage of wheat and other grains, would act with dispatch.
The reason we are in the position in which we are is that in the 1950 crop there was a great deal of damp and tough wheat, the difference being two to three per cent in extra moisture. That wheat was stored in the elevators on the prairies. Those elevators were not cleared out and when this present crop came along many of the elevators were full or half full with wheat from the previous year. Nothing effective was done on the part of the wheat board or the government to meet a situation that every farmer realized was facing the west. We in the opposition asked over and over again that something be done. I oan remember my hon. friends to the left asking for the appointment of a transport controller throughout the year 1951. But nothing was done until August. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) asked for that several times and the answer given was one of indifference and apathy.
All through the fall we in this house endeavoured to bring to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government the terrible prospect in western Canada. Too many of our freight cars were in the United States and there was a great shortage of cars, particularly on the Canadian Pacific lines. There were no available storage facilities in the line elevators. We asked that something be done to provide payment to the farmers for storage so that he could arrange his own storage facilities, but nothing was done.
Now we find ourselves in the prairies with 28 per cent of all wheat, and 24 per cent of all oats and barley as damp or tough. We find 28 per cent of Saskatchewan wheat and barley still unharvested on the farm, with the percentage being 33 per cent in Alberta, and 6 per cent in Manitoba. The total figures exceed a hundred millions of bushels.
The elevators are glutted. Surely action is demanded even at this late date. The loss is going to be severe. It would have been much better had the government realized the situation earlier. I suggest certain action now. I would say that there should be a conference, not only of the provinces but of the dominion and representatives of the elevator companies. I know there was a conference in Regina recently but that (* onf ere nee could not act because it did not have the power.
The time has come to arrange further markets for this wheat. We should do under the Colombo plan what we have done for

Mr. Speaker, I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) as to the steps the government might consider and take in regard to the redistribution of the representation in this House of Commons. It seems to me that a province such as Saskatchewan, which contains approximately 40 per cent of all the cultivated land in Canada, cannot be adequately represented by any fewer than the twenty members now representing it. The hon. member for Lake Centre has said it is his understanding that members from Saskatchewan belonging to all parties are agreed that our representation in parliament should not be reduced and that certainly it should not be reduced by five seats, or the equivalent of 25 per cent.
The Address-Mr. Argue
The Regina Leader-Post has given a good deal of thought and study to the matter of adequate representation for Saskatchewan. In an excellent editorial on January 17, which followed an editorial of a month previous along the same lines, it advanced what I feel were sound arguments in support of the proposition that the number of Saskatchewan seats should not be reduced. I do not intend to read that editorial, but I would like to quote one short paragraph from it:
The proposal advanced recently by this newspaper has since been widely endorsed that there should be a deviation from the representation by population in the House of Commons to forestall the threatened loss of five members of parliament by Saskatchewan and one by Manitoba.
The editorial goes on to point out that if Saskatchewan had within its boundaries a Montreal or Toronto, or some large city, by making the ridings within the urban areas a good deal larger by standard of population, the rural constituencies could be kept down to a manageable size, to an area that members could adequately represent. I think our problem in Saskatchewan is somewhat different from that of rural members in other provinces. In southwest Saskatchewan there are farmers in every part of the whole area. In some of the northern areas you get huge spaces where no one or almost no one lives. Within the settled part of Saskatchewan there are people on almost every section of land, and certainly people in every township. A member attempting to represent a rural constituency must travel thousands upon thousands of miles by car if he is to even partially cover his constituency.
I believe the government should consider the appointment of a royal commission to look into the matter of representation, to consider what representation each province should have by way of a floor. If we had representation by population purely and simply in Canada now perhaps there would be no argument, but other provinces and other areas have operative floors. The people of western Canada believe they too should be given a floor to provide them with some protection as to the number of representatives they will have in this parliament.
I have risen tonight chiefly to make a plea for a new deal, a square deal for western agriculture. I believe .there is room and need for many important improvements in present legislation. The old age pensioner should get an increase now, and in my opinion a $20 per month increase is necessary to provide an adequate pension. Then a year from now, if inflation has continued, that $60 should be increased by an appropriate amount.

An hon. member reminds me that free hospitalization and medical care are also provided to certain of our pensioners in the province of Saskatchewan.
I go from a suggested improvement in old age pensions to improvements which I feel should be made in health facilities for the people of Canada. In 1945 the federal government laid down proposals to the provinces for a complete health insurance scheme. The people of Canada have waited seven years for the federal government to do anything substantial in the way of implementing that program. I believe the federal government should now offer the people of Canada a complete health program in co-operation with the provinces so that any province that is willing to co-operate in such a program can provide complete hospital and medical care for the people within that province.
In Saskatchewan we have a hospitalization program which, to put it moderately, is second to none. We have not yet gone far enough. We have a hospitalization program coupled with certain other medical benefits for all the people in Saskatchewan, but we would like to be able to provide a complete medical service now for all the people of our province. If the federal government would offer, as it did in 1945, concrete proposals whereby the federal government would co-operate with the province of Saskatchewan, we would have complete medical service in a short time. I want to tell the members of this house that we in Saskatchewan have not gone as far as we want to go in the way of providing better medical services. We feel that the federal government should adopt its own 1945 proposals and put them in legislative form. If the federal government does not bring in legislation to co-operate with the provinces in a health program, the people of Saskatchewan are not going to stand still. I say that, irrespective of political complexion, the people of Saskatchewan are a progressive people and are going to provide medical services step by step, even if the federal government continues to sit on its fat surplus and do nothing about a medical program.

I turn now to the third point in social security legislation which I believe should be improved. I have never spoken about family allowances without giving the federal government, under the leadership of Mackenzie King, along with the other members of parliament, full credit for bringing in the Family Allowances Act of 1944. I still give them full credit for having done that. This act provided a minimum payment of $5 per month and a maximum payment of $8 per month for each child. But since 1945, by allowing inflation to run wild, the government has gradually whittled down the purchasing power of that allowance by at least 40 per cent. If the federal government were to do no more now than to bring in an amendment to the Family Allowances Act which would restore the purchasing power of the family allowance, it would have to provide for an immediate increase of more than 60 per cent.
I give the government full credit for having introduced family allowances, but merely having introduced it is not good enough. I have on the order paper now a resolution in my name asking that family allowances be increased to the point that the 1945 purchasing power be restored. If that were done to an extent necessary to provide the same purchasing power as the allowance had when first introduced in 1944, the minimum family allowance payment would have to be increased from $5 to $8 per month and the maximum from $8 to $13 per month per child.
The government always says, where is the money going to come from? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has a fairly healthy surplus of some $721 million. He says it is going to be cut in half by the end of the present fiscal year, but there is a surplus. Before this session is completed the minister will be given one hundred ideas as to how that surplus might be spent but I can see no better way than by the government improving the old age pensions, making provision for a complete health program and increasing family allowances. I know it would take some more money than the surplus alone to bring into effect all the suggestions I have made. I am sure that it would. The Minister of Finance-and I give him credit for this-was nevertheless able to devise a 2-2-2 formula for meeting the nomeans-test old age pension: 2 per cent more income tax, 2 per cent more corporation tax and 2 per cent of the existing sales tax earmarked for the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act. I do not think that 2-2-2 formula is really going to hurt anybody in Canada, but the revenue derived from it
The Address-Mr. Argue is going to help a great many elderly Canadian citizens, particularly because of the present inflationary period.
I for one believe that the finances necessary for a better social security program could be raised, to the extent of whatever is needed in addition to the surplus that now exists, that the Canadian people would be willing to pay whatever increased taxes may be necessary. What the people of Canada are asking for is some leadership from this government and for an opportunity to pay in to an over-all social security program that will provide them with some real security in the way of a better old age pension program, a health program for all, and increased family allowances.
I turn now from that subject, Mr. Speaker, in order to dwell for a short time on the things I feel that the farmers of western Canada need at the present time. In the past I have from time to time advanced various ideas in the house. Many of those ideas the government has not accepted.
I can, however, name one or two that they have accepted, and I am glad they have done so. I refer, first of all, to their allowing farmers to deduct from their income fees paid to farmers' unions. I think that is a good thing, and I am glad the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) made that announcement the other day.
During the debate last year on the Canadian Wheat Board Act I proposed an amendment asking that the government wind up any oat, wheat or barley pool period within sixty days of the end of the pool period. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that he could not accept my amendment. He said the legislation as it was drafted was merely to handle dribs and drabs, a few thousand bushels of wheat here and there, or a few thousand bushels of other grain. I was glad, however, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce closed out the oat, wheat and barley pool even though, by so doing, he had to transfer some tens of millions of bushels, and that the final payments were made within a few months of the end of the crop year. I think he followed a good business practice by closing out those pools and paying out to farmers the money that rightly belongs to them. The minister has himself established a precedent that I hope he will continue to follow. While he was not willing to put into legislative form my suggested amendment, I was nevertheless pleased to see that, in practice, he adopted it.

As the hon. member for Lake Centre said this evening, one of the present problems- one that now amounts almost to a calamity for western farmers-is the matter of damp grain. The hon. member for Lake Centre outlined a number of suggestions that, as he said, probably would help to relieve this situation. I have not time to refer to those suggestions, but I think the government has overlooked one important method by which a great deal of this grain might be salvaged. I refer to the small grain drier.
By means of questions from this group and from other opposition groups, we attempted to get grain driers allowed in last fall duty free, but we did not succeed; but grain driers now come in duty free if they are to be used and kept in Canada. The board of grain commissioners and the Minister of Trade and Commerce last week pooh-poohed the idea that local farm grain driers were of any real value. May I say that there are two different types of grain driers. One that has been used is a large, expensive commercial grain drier, used in commerce to dry chemicals for the chemical industry. It is true that it is practically valueless for drying grain, certainly in its normal method of operation. Then there is the small grain drier, one that is produced in Nebraska. It has passed with flying colours all of the tests that I have read of in the press. It is able to dry fairly substantial quantities of grain and in good condition. I think that the board of grain commissioners should have inquired into these various farm grain driers, should have put them to proper tests and should have made a scientific appraisal of their value. Once having appraised their value, they should have promoted their use to as large an extent as possible.
I have a great deal of confidence in the ingenuity of the local farmer. If he were given some direction and encouragement, I believe he would be able to adapt for his own use a grain drier that might be extremely useful in saving his grain. But instead of making proper inquiries, sending out literature, and explaining to the farmers how the grain might best be dried on the farms, press statements went out from time to time saying: Beware of farm driers; farm driers are ruining the grain. Even the minister himself the other day said that in his opinion farm driers have no read place in this emergency. I think that a mistake was made in that regard by the Department of Trade and Commerce and by its agencies.
It will soon be time for Canada and other countries in the world to negotiate once again -as I hope they will-an international wheat agreement. We have had some experiences

with the British wheat agreement and with the present international wheat agreement. The farmers of western Canada are not at all satisfied with the treatment they received. They felt that they were entitled to a 25cent payment as a final payment on the five-year pool. They still think, as I do, that they are entitled to another $48 million at least, being 30 cents a bushel on the 160 million bushels of wheat sold in Canada to domestic consumers within that five-year period at a price below the price to Great Britain. When that debate was in progress, Mr. Speaker, we in this group attempted to have parliament approve a motion asking for a 25-cent a bushel payment, but Liberal members at that time turned the motion down. Last year it was my pleasure to ask, by way of a motion, for a $2 final payment, that is to provide a total price for the 1950 crop of $2 a bushel. I think that was a moderate request. I think it was a price that was probably still considerably less than parity. But once again, Mr. Speaker, Liberal members, exercising their judgment, decided to vote down that motion.
One of the worst features of the government's policy now with regard to wheat is the continued forced subsidization by western farmers of Canadian consumers because the price of domestic wheat is held to the international wheat agreement price.
Class II wheat today is over $2.30 a bushel. It has been up to $2.40 a bushel or more. Canadian consumers paid $2 a bushel for Canadian wheat in the last two years of the British wheat agreement and are today paying $1.80 per bushel. Since that time though the cost of production has gone up the government has continued its policy of forcing the wheat farmer to subsidize the consumer in Canada. I think it is time the government changed its policy so that the Canadian consumer would be removed from the back of the wheat farmer. I do not ask for higher prices for bread, or that the consumer be forced to pay a higher price for domestic wheat; but I do feel that any subsidizing of wheat should be done by the federal government. It should not be a subsidy extracted by the government from the wheat producers of western Canada.
Some mention was made this afternoon as to the government's policy on floor prices, particularly in view of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. We in this group have always supported a parity price. We believe that the Agricultural Prices Support Act, with the $200 million that was to be appropriated for the purposes of that act, could and should be used to provide fair floor prices for farmers from one end of Canada to the other.

But what has the government's policy been with relation to floor prices? When the floor drops out of any agricultural product, and the price goes so low that production is discouraged the Minister of Agriculture then comes in and establishes what he calls a floor under the commodity concerned. For instance, the floor price, so-called, under eggs is 38 cents a dozen. It means to the farmer in my area who produces eggs a price of 25 cents a dozen-and that even when the mercury reaches 35 or 40 degrees below zero.
That is not an adequate floor price. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture have asked for a floor price of 44 cents a dozen. In the debate last fall-I believe it was December 17-the Minister of Agriculture said that the floor price under hogs at that time was $32.50 a hundredweight for Wiltshire sides at Halifax. That would mean $27.50 a hundredweight, dressed, at Winnipeg. That was not an adequate floor price, and the farmers said to the minister that they should have something better. Instead of the minister announcing a more adequate floor price, the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), who was then Acting Minister of Agriculture, announced on February 16 of this year a new floor at $26 for grade A hogs at the public stockyards in Toronto and Montreal. I see in the most recent issue of the Free Press that the price for hogs at Winnipeg is $24.50 a hundredweight.
In other words the floor has been lowered. The government has changed the floor price and, instead of improving it, because of the increased cost of production, has once again reduced that floor.
Now we are faced with the calamity of the foot-and-mouth disease, with provincial and the United States embargo barriers placed against the movement of livestock. Once again the market price to the farmer is in great jeopardy. What has the government offered the farmer by way of a proper floor price at this time? Absolutely nothing.
In announcing the price the Minister of Resources and Development said in part:
It is not in the interests of producers to allow unsaleable surpluses to develop, and should it be found that the policy was having such an effect, it would be reviewed.
Surpluses may well develop now, in the light of the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak and the closing off of the American market to Canadian livestock. What is the promise by the government to the farmers of Canada? It is that if the hog surplus increases they are going to review the present floor price,
The Address-Mr. Argue with that in mind. To me that means only one thing, and that is another reduction in the floor price under hogs.

What is more, as a result we have lost part of our export market. The tobacco growers have already agreed to decrease their acreage by one-third. That is not a healthy situation. Possibly the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance has visited that area and has learned about the smaller incomes these people are going to get. Possibly the Prime Minister knew that, when he said we are not going to decrease taxes next year. I have no hesitation in saying tonight that the only way the government is going to recoup the revenue lost in connection with the cigarette industry because of increased smuggling and the smaller consumption of Canadian cigarettes is if the tax is reduced so that a package of twenty cigarettes will sell for 30 cents for say a period of a year. I do not say how much longer they should remain at that price but I cannot see for one minute how this industry, which has meant so much to the economy of Canada, will be revived otherwise. We have been two decades building up the tobacco industry and it has been shattered, you might say, in one year.
There are other matters I should like to discuss if I have time but now I want to make a few other observations. A suggestion I should like to make, and one which I think warrants the consideration of the members of this house, has to do with the advisability of referring estimates presented to parliament to a committee for detailed study. Through such action it would be possible to bring before such a committee senior civil servants of the Department of Finance and other departments, and thereby give members of the house the opportunity to ascertain the premises and forecasts upon which taxation proposals are based. I make this observation before I get into the meat of my argument for obvious reasons. Experience in the past years has shown that there has been a definite tendency to underestimate the gross national production, the gross national income, and the consumer turnover in Canada, and this has resulted in the forecasts of revenues by the Minister of Finance being very considerably under the actual revenues received.

I agree that it is nice to have a buoyant economy which results in nearly full employment and production greater than anticipated, but the fact remains that members of this house, when they authorize the levy of taxes on the Canadian people, should have more information as to the anticipated tempo of business upon which these taxes are to be levied. Members should know certain things. Will the gross national production in Canada in 1952 be in the neighbourhood of $22 billion, $23 billion or $24 billion? Will the gross national income be in the neighbourhood of $18 billion, as now forecast, or will it be $19 billion?
Only by having access to the best information available in this field can members of the house conscientiously say that the tax levels proposed by the Minister of Finance are reasonable and will result in raising the revenue to cover the expenditures voted by parliament.
One thing further such a committee could do would be to ascertain from those responsible in the various departments the full extent of efforts made to curtail or defer unnecessary non-defence expenditures at this time. We were assured by the Minister of Finance in his last budget speech that nondefence expenditures would be deferred. According to the last financial report available to us from the comptroller of the treasury, covering the first nine months of the present fiscal year, these non-defence expenditures, which were to be curtailed in view of the heavy burden of our rearmament, show an increase of $37-4 million, even after allowance was made in the estimates for the increased cost of old age and blind pensions, family allowances and other essential services which -must be maintained. If we are to take an effective step to curtail non-defence expenditures in this country, that step must be taken when the estimates are brought before this house and before the expenditures are made, not two or three years later when the facts become known through the public accounts. Do you know what this reminds me of, Mr. Speaker? A little boy was having his breakfast and left two prunes on his plate. His mother said: "I want you to eat those prunes; they are good for you."
The Address-Mr. Murphy He refused, so she said, "If you don't eat the prunes I will tell God on you". Just then it began to thunder, with lightning to beat the band, and the little boy went to the window and said, "That's an awful fuss you are making, God, over two prunes."
Since parliament convened we have been told by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that the Canadian people cannot expect very much in the way of tax reductions in the coming fiscal year. The reason advanced as to why it is necessary to continue the present high level of taxation is the uncertain international situation. On the surface this looks like a plausible reason. Unfortunately, however, analysis of the facts of our financial structure does not bear out the necessity for continued high taxation. When the present excessively high taxation levels were established by the Minister of Finance in his budget of April 10, 1951, they were set to yield, we were told, a surplus of $30 million. They were set on an anticipated gross national production of $20 billion, on a forecast gross national income of $16-5 billion or thereabouts, and on a forecast consumer turnover of approximately $12 billion. It now turns out that these forecasts were considerably short. The gross national production, instead of $20 billion, was $21-5 billion. The gross national income, instead of $16-5 billion, turned out to be more than $17 billion. The consumer turnover, instead of $12 billion, turned out to be more than $13 billion.
As a result the forecast of a surplus of $30 million has now been exceeded many times, even after making due allowance for the inability of the government to spend all they budgeted for with regard to defence, something they were told during the budget debate last year they would be unable to do. Now we are told by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that it will be necessary to continue these high levels of taxation except in certain individual cases where adjustments may be necessary, no doubt because of the unemployment which has arisen as a direct result of excessive taxation and its effects upon markets. Today the forecast of gross national production in Canada for the coming year is $23 billion, as -compared with $20 billion a year ago when these taxation levels were set. The forecast for gross national income is $18 billion, as compared to the less than $17 billion when the Minister of Finance said these high levels of taxation were necessary. For this year the consumer turnover is estimated at $14 billion, as against the $12 billion forecast a year ago.

The Address-Mr. Murphy
It is obvious, therefore, that if the present rates of taxation, which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance say may be continued, resulted in a surplus of $700 million for the first nine months of the present fiscal year, and allowing for additional expenditures which may come in the last few months of the present year, to continue those levels on the increased forecasts for 1952 could not help but result in a surplus of hundreds of millions of dollars for the next fiscal year.
The Minister of Finance tells us that he was wrong, perhaps, but that it was a good thing because the money has been used for the retirement of debt. Recently in a broadcast his parliamentary assistant said this retirement of debt was a brave thing. Never once did the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary assistant stand up in this parliament and say, "I propose to levy high taxation on the people of Canada, at a time when they are burdened with the highest cost of living in their lives, for the purpose of debt reduction." I would say this is budgeting under false pretences. Debt reduction as a fiscal policy is all right in its place, but there is a time and place for it. Debt reduction as a fiscal policy of this government should be on the authority of this parliament. If the Minister of Finance wants to continue his high level of taxation at this time for the purpose of debt reduction, then when he brings down his budget it will be his responsibility to obtain the endorsation of this parliament for that purpose.
Further, in view of the increased forecast for 1952 gross national production, gross national income and consumer turnover, and the direct relationship this bears to the system of indirect and regressive taxation built up by this government, this parliament must give serious consideration to the taxation proposals of the minister when he brings down his budget. At the present time in this country our indirect taxes are rapidly climbing to a point equal to our direct taxes. Many of these indirect or hidden taxes, such as the 25 per cent increase in the sales tax this government brought in a year ago, are regressive taxes which have a direct detrimental effect upon the cost of living in this country.
I am quite in accord with the belief that Canada should play its full part in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I am aware that this is going to cost this country a considerable sum of money and that this commitment must be met as far as possible out of taxation. But in view of the fact that during the present year this country was 
unable to spend the money for defence and for rearmament which this parliament voted, caution should be exercised in the coming budget in order to not again overestimate our expenditures simply for the purpose of creating among our people and among our allies a false sense of security. Otherwise the levels of taxation will be set on a basis which cannot help but result in huge surpluses extracted from the people of Canada at a time when they are experiencing the highest cost of living in their history; and further, extracted from business in this country at a time when we are experiencing the greatest industrial expansion in history, when those same Canadian enterprises should be able to invest in the expansion of Canada, were they left enough from their earnings after paying the taxes that are levied upon them. This point was very ably emphasized this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell).
Today we are fortunate in that we are receiving a very much accelerated inflow of capital for development purposes. I welcome this as necessary for the development of this country. I would point out, however, that existing Canadian enterprises should be participating in this development to a greater extent than is the case today. We welcome this United States and other capital into this country for development purposes. We are receiving this capital in Canada because we have given the assurance that both the capital and the earnings can be withdrawn if and when desired. Should that demand for withdrawal of capital come at a time when our imports exceed our exports, the demand for gold and foreign exchange to meet the commitment could be a serious drain on the Canadian economy.
It would seem to me advisable that as much Canadian capital as possible should be available for investment in the industrial expansion of this nation, because in that way we will considerably reduce the future drain on gold or foreign exchange in this country as the earnings from that invested capital become available for distribution. This possibility is by no means remote, because today, were it not for the inflow of capital to this country to counterbalance our excess of imports over exports, our dollar and gold reserve position would be under serious strain.
It is perfectly evident from the statement of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that no election is planned for this year. We recall what happened prior to 1949-it has been referred to more than once today-when the taxpayers were told of the

great reduction in taxation this government was able to accomplish. These reductions in taxes should come this year, and not be held back to suit the convenience of the Liberal party's political machine in this country. That is what happened in 1949, and we want no repetition of that in 1953 or 1954. I believe we should have finished with this political budgeting.
One admission that both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) have made, however, is that certain adjustments are necessary in the present taxation level. It was almost impossible to escape that admission. As a result of this excessive taxation today, or what the parliamentary assistant (Mr. Sinclair) calls "this brave fiscal policy", we have pockets of unemployment in the textile industry, the automobile industry, the electrical goods industry, and there are forecasts of other pockets rapidly developing in other phases of our economy. We have the spectacle of the Minister of Finance putting on this exorbitant, ill-advised tobacco tax and handing the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) a taxation measure which, in effect, is proving unenforceable. It is resulting in smuggling in this country reminiscent of the days of bootlegging. It is just one example of the dangers involved in excessive taxation which was expected to result in increased revenues, but which has acted in reverse.
Another problem of vital interest to the Canadian people resulting from excessive federal taxation is the situation arising within the municipalities of this country. Today, municipal authorities are finding it extremely difficult to operate under the revenues available to them. I believe almost every member will agree with that statement. Excessive taxation at the federal level, and particularly the hidden or turnover taxes, is levied on the very people who have the responsibility of meeting the obligations involved in our municipal structure of government. Today in most of our larger centres the demand for housing creates the necessity for heavy expenditures to provide the services essential to any housing project.
Another rapidly increasing burden is the cost of education. I very much fear that unless this problem is faced, first by the federal authorities where the initial action must be taken, the municipalities are going to be forced into demanding the right to levy a sales tax or some other indirect or hidden tax in order to meet their obligations. Should that situation arise in this country and we experience an extension of these regressive forms of indirect taxation, the
The Address-Mr. Murphy obligations on an individual Canadian home owner or a businessman, as a large municipal taxpayer, will be very serious.
In all probability, Mr. Speaker, there will be meetings this year between the dominion and those provinces that have not already signed the dominion-provincial agreement. Coming from a municipality which is developing rapidly-I think that applies to many municipalities in this country-I should like to say that the municipal viewpoint should be seriously considered in those meetings. In most areas taxation levels are so high that it does not pay to own property. Most members will agree with me that these taxes are bound to increase as our population and industrial development increase. It seems to me that, so far as the province of Ontario is concerned in any event, the predicament of these municipalities should be seriously considered. We know that over the last few years the federal government has been taking an increasingly large share of revenue from our national income, and at the expense of the lower levels of government, particularly the municipal level.
I do hope that when these agreements are under consideration there will be no restrictions imposed upon municipalities resorting to other forms of taxation, as has been done in other agreements. The federal government is taking such a large share of the revenue that the municipalities are badly handicapped. I believe it is well known that such a restriction is contained in those agreements already signed and, with one or two exceptions, no municipality will have the authority to raise additional revenue. I am not advocating that municipalities should impose sales taxes, but I do say that the predicament in which these municipalities find themselves should be considered.
I wish to take a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, to deal with a situation that exists in my riding as well as some other ridings in the Dominion of Canada. In Sarnia we are proud to have the great Polymer Corporation, which is of great importance to the people of this country as well as the other democratic nations with whom we are allied. In the autumn session of 1949 we had before us the Abbott formula for payments by crown companies in lieu of taxes. We all welcomed that, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think there was a member in this house who could possibly object to the fairness of the formula. I say that because I know the minister will not consider our exchange of a few minutes ago as anything other than good fun.
Any industry in any municipality brings with it a responsibility to supply services such

If perchance the mayor did not know, as he should have, for I told him and sent him the formula, that they were subject to tax, I think that a responsible and fair government and a fair executive should say:	We are
responsible and we will pay our fair share. I should like to see that this matter receives the consideration which it deserves not only in the city of Sarnia but elsewhere and that the same fair principle be applied to any crown company from coast to coast in this country of ours.

Mr. Speaker, the year 1951 was a historic one for immigration in this country. I take the occasion to congratulate the minister and the government upon the excellent record of bringing into this country last year approximately
200.000	immigrants. The previous bumper year was in 1913 when we brought in 400,000 immigrants, and in 1928 when we brought in
166.000	immigrants. My purpose in rising was to indicate support to the government so that our immigration policy will not be a flash in the pan but rather that we shall encourage the government to continue bringing immigrants into this country in large numbers.
I said that 1951 was the biggest year since 1913. That statement sounds impressive until we look at the figures in the intervening years. Then we realize that, forty years ago, we admitted to this country more than twice as many people as we admitted in 1951. I think it is interesting for the house to know what happened to those 200,000 immigrants. The exact figure is 194,391. Of this number 114,786 are workers. The rest are dependents. They increased the working force in Canada by 2 per cent. Of that number, 25,890 went to the farms; 33,682 were skilled workers; 6,531 were domestics and 31,007 were unskilled and semi-skilled persons who did little to aggravate our present seasonal unemployment. There are those in our country who say we should cut down immigration and that we cannot absorb such an inflow as we had in the year 1951. I think it is our duty in this house to show them that they are wrong.
Time and again it has been proven that immigration benefits a country. Immigrants do

not take jobs; they make jobs. I am greatly impressed by an argument that was used by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris). This was the argument. It is that in 1949-50 the unemployment peak was higher than the peak this year, although the number of immigrants brought in during 1949 was approximately 100,000 less than the number brought in in 1951. While I am at it I think I might as well clear up what is in the minds of a great number, if not all, of the members of this house. It should be remembered that even during the height of our economic activity there were between 150,000 and 250,000 persons seasonally unemployed each winter in this country.
In the face of this knowledge that I have given the house, I wanted to make the house aware of the fact that from 1945 to 1950 immigrants have brought to this country $300 million in new capital, have established 75 industries providing at least 6,000 new jobs. Our worst unemployment periods were from 1931 to 1940 when we had no immigration. Our highest employment in the early part of the century was when we had a record amount of immigration. I think it is true that immigrants cannot be absorbed as easily today as they were in the days when we had land available for everyone. Yet work on the land is available today to the extent of the 20,000 that are needed immediately on the farms of this country. We are now an industrial economy; it is a little different from an agricultural economy. Our immigrants need to be placed rather than absorbed. All that the immigrant asks is that he be accepted and that he be understood. Immigrants are not asking for impressive receptions or a protected relationship. They are lonely people who come to this new environment, these new conditions, trying to make a new life for themselves and to become Canadians as quickly as possible.
We cannot move forward in our economic development without the addition annually to our population of a large number of the same kind of people who have in the past demonstrated their skill, their ability, and their loyalty to this country. We are one of the world's major trading nations. We used to be third in the export-import market; we are now fourth. France has recently jumped ahead of us; and present figures indicate that Germany is breathing down our neck. Canada is first in exports and imports, on a per capita basis. Nevertheless, I think it is important that we should, if it is at all possible, win back our former position of third greatest trading nation in the world rather than the fourth. To accomplish that purpose we 55704-19
The Address-Mr. Croll need more people. There are some people who are blaming the immigrants for unemployment. Immigrants are not to blame for that temporary condition. Some were being so unkind as to blame the immigrants for the hoof-and-mouth disease. It is extremely easy to make scapegoats of them because they are not in a good position to defend themselves unless we, as members of the house, speak up for them and for justice. They too suffer through unemployment.
Any talk of flooding this country with cheap labour is unworthy of those people who are telling that tale. The workers benefits, whether they are union benefits or non-union, are the concern of all of us in the house, and are zealously guarded. I have not heard of any evidence that any of the immigrants have been under-cutting the market.
I think it would be interesting for the house to know what I think is labour's traditional position on the immigration policy. Labour has always supported immigration, with the following provisos: That immigration will not reduce the standard of living of the workers who have worked so hard to achieve that standard; that there will not be created in this country a pool of cheap and docile labour; that the immigration policy is designed to develop the resources of this country so as to give additional work to our own people.
That is my understanding of their position, and that I understand is the government's policy. I think there should be a meeting of minds on that. I point this out further to the unions: the majority of those who are at present coming in as immigrants are from countries where trade unions are old, strong and powerful-perhaps not quite as democratic in some of the countries as are our trade unions. But here is an opportunity for the unions to enlist them; here is new blood to help them hold the gains that they have already made and which from time to time of course they will improve.
Unemployment in this country at the moment is a problem. In the main it is seasonal. Some part of it is due to the temporary saturation of the markets in some of our industries, some of it is due to the reluctance on the part of manufacturers to reduce their margins of profit. Credit restrictions to control inflation and, to some extent, excise taxes, have had some effect.

I have said that credit restrictions to control inflation and excise taxes to some extent have had some effect. Production dislocation arising out of defence production and a shortage of materials in some industries- all of these have contributed to some extent to unemployment. I believe that all that will soon pass, already there are signs of its passing. In the interval there is provision made for people who are unemployed, though I must agree that unemployment insurance is no substitute for a job. And was never meant to be.
But those people who say that we ought to bring over to this country only those people we can immediately place are saying only, in effect, that we ought to move the national employment service to some cities in Europe, when we need twenty carpenters that we ask for twenty carpenters, and bring them in, and when we need twenty bricklayers that we bring them over.
Well, that is not an immigration policy; that will not build up our country. I wonder if the anti-immigrationists believe that Canada is already overcrowded, when we have a land area greater than the United States but have only one-tenth of its population. Canada is just the reverse of the old woman who lived in a shoe: We have so few children we don't know what to do. We are a country of wide-open spaces, and we have not even begun to fill them.
I often wonder why we live in fear of things to come, and why we do not face such problems as immigration with courage and with confidence. I will admit that the city of Toronto is getting a bit crowded. But can we say the same thing for the province of Ontario or the province of Alberta?
I dug up some interesting figures. I shall now repeat them slowly because I believe they are very interesting. They show that prior to 1930, 53 per cent of the immigrants that came to this country went to the prairie provinces and British Columbia, 40 per cent went to Ontario and Quebec and 7 per cent to the maritime provinces. In 1951, 55 per cent of the immigrants came to Ontario, 22 per cent to Quebec, thus giving the two central provinces 77 per cent of the immigrants. Instead of the 53 per cent they had prior to 1930, the prairie provinces and British Columbia received only 13 per cent, and the maritime provinces 10 per cent.
That is a reversal of the historic trend in this country. Not only will it bring to us economic headaches but, as was indicated from the floor of the house tonight, we see the political problems it is raising in our country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How many of those immigrants stayed in Canada? The hon. member told us the number who had gone to Ontario and other parts of Canada in recent years. How many remained in Canada?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Later on 1 shall give the figure showing how many have gone to the United States, but I cannot tell whether or not they were immigrants. Probably not. It is not possible to give that figure, because I do not think they are kept in that way. However, I shall give the figures asked for at a later point in my speech.
Those who are opposed to immigration want us to believe that in this country there are just so many jobs, so many homes, so many apartments, so many suits of clothes, so many pairs of shoes, and so many loaves of bread. They reason that if we admit more people there will not be enough to go around. Yet at the same time there are more people employed in this country today than ever before.
Returning to the subject of population for a moment: The population of Canada is a little more than 14 million. In the last ten years there has been an increase of 2,502,774, or 21-8 per cent. Only British Columbia is well above the national average. Ontario and Quebec are just at the national average. The over-all increase in population in the prairie provinces in ten years has been 4-7 per cent; in Alberta it has been 17-6 per cent, in Manitoba, 5-8 per cent, and in Saskatchewan there has been a loss of 7 [DOT] 5 per cent. British Columbia has had an increase of 41 per cent, Ontario has increased by 20-5 per cent, Quebec by 20-4 per cent, the maritime provinces by 9-8 per cent.
Speaking of the prairie provinces particularly, we have there a total area of 753,497 square miles inhabited by 2,537,549 people, occupying an area half the size of India with a population half the size of Switzerland. Today a nation more than twice as large in population as it was in 1913, and many times as strong, is taking in only half the number of immigrants we took in at that time. I merely point out to the house that it is time we burst these bonds of caution. We have to take a firm stand in this country on immigration because we can produce more homes, more suits of clothing, more pairs of shoes and more loaves of bread. All that increased activity will make for more jobs. The answer to that is more people.
Has Canada progressed since 1900? It has, because we have more than three times the population we had at the beginning of the century. We have used wisely and intelligently our natural resources and we have taken advantage of our opportunities. Unless

we continue to increase our population we shall not continue to grow and prosper. I think we should set our sights at 25 million, and I do not mean at the end of the century. Our population experts in the bureau of statistics can tell us what Canada's natural increase will be in the next twenty years. The difference between that figure and 25 million can be made up only in one way, that is by immigration. We can achieve that by an all-out effort.
I am convinced that the country wants more of the right kind of immigration, the kind that we have been getting particularly this year. Dozens of important representative bodies have gone on record during the last five years to that effect. I do not deny that quite a large number of people have come to Canada. Every one of them has been a welcome addition to this country. From 1945 to 1950 Canada admitted 568,000 immigrants, an average of 95,000 a year. I now give my friend the figure he asked for. During that same period 314,600 persons left Canada, by the back door I think, to go to the United States or to other places. Our net total gain was 268,100. Who those people are I have no way of knowing, nor has the bureau of statistics, but those are the figures I was able to obtain and I think they are authentic.
Does anyone seriously contend that these new Canadians have not benefited this country and themselves? It is just common logic that we can absorb and profitably use many more. People are the greatest asset that any country could have.

My argument of course is that if we have the people here we can use our own raw materials and do our own manufacturing. What we need in this country is an added perspective, one that will take a 55704-191
The Address-Mr. Croll good look at the sweeping panorama of the years that lie ahead, one that will show such short-term problems as unemployment and economic upheaval against the long-term goal of a nation living up to its destiny and its potential. Birth and growth call for some degree of pain. Those who cry out against large-scale immigration are unmindful of something we have heard repeated often in this house and this country but which appears sometimes to have lost its significance, that the true wealth of a country is its people.
It is a little strange that some people should be concerned about the arrival of immigrants in Canada. It seems to me that the time to start worrying is when people do not want to come to this country. A few years ago Canadians could look at well-established frontiers of their country and marvel at the space available for millions of newcomers. Since the war we have uncovered a fabulous new frontier in the northwest, we have added an island province, we have pushed our northeastern frontiers beyond Quebec into the rediscovered Labrador. Our mineral and agricultural frontiers have opened up beyond our dreams. This is the time for immigrants, if ever we needed them. For without people the fields are fallow, the factories are idle and the mines and forests are useless.
I want to say one word particularly with respect to British immigration. I think these figures will be found interesting. Until 1925, 62 per cent of our immigrants were British; by 1948 the percentage had fallen to 35; by 1951 it had fallen to 17. I think at this time we should examine the situation to find out the reason why British immigrants do not come and what we can do to correct a situation which needs correcting. I am one of those who hold the opinion that we shall regret it in the days to come if we do not sufficiently stock this country with British people.
First, of course, are the restrictions on money. The British do not permit much money to leave their country. Then the British government is not too helpful when it comes to immigration. They do not want to lose their skilled people and technicians, that is the kind of people for whom we have the greatest attraction. I know a firm in Toronto that brought over a couple of hundred skilled people. They sent to England, brought them to this country, paid them good salaries under contract. They no sooner completed their contract, the Americans came over and offered almost double the salaries. They left. The firm in Toronto could not possibly match the salaries that were offered.

The Address-Mr. Croll
I think the government can do a little more than they have done with respect to British immigration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At the present time the government advances four-fifths of the fare of the head of the family only. The family must wait in England until the father or the head repays the four-fifths of the fare the government has advanced and has earned enough money to pay the full fare for the rest of his family. Our scheme is very attractive to single people, but it is not so attractive to family people, and they are the kind we want.
As against that we have to match what Australia offers. Australia will transport all members of a family on payment of $30 per head. They pay the balance. It is a gift which does not need to be repaid. The result is that many immigrants who want to keep their families together are going to Australia. Last year we obtained 13,427 British immigrants and during the same time Australia obtained 75,000. As I have said, ours is a good plan for single men but it does not help the family man. Another difficulty about immigration is the shortage of transport between Great Britain and Canada. It is easier to get transport from the continent than it is from Britain. We are able to charter vessels which do not meet British requirements but do meet continental needs. I think it is well for the house to know that it is easier to bring immigrants to Canada in the wintertime because transport is available, the tourist traffic is not quite so heavy. During the summertime it is very difficult to obtain transport. Consequently we sometimes find ourselves, when we are subject to seasonal unemployment, with more immigrants on our hands than we can readily handle, but that is a passing phase.
Last year we spent $6 million to assist British immigrants whereas Australia spent $40 million. The difficulty of course is that we have a revolving fund of $6 million and when the $6 million is used up there is no further assistance for these immigrants. Last year the fund ran short in November, and during November and December there was no money available for immigrants.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No immigration policy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Something special should be done with respect to British immigration which all of us in this house want to encourage as much as possible.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Could the hon. member give us the same comparative figures for British immigration with respect to Australia and Canada for 1946 and 1947?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I can give the figures for all immigrants but I cannot give the figures for British immigrants. I thought this particular year would prove my point. I repeat, what good after all are all our natural resources, what good are our industries and what good are our millions of acres of land unless we have in Canada hands to work them, to consume their production and to share our obligations, both national and international? To oppose immigration is against reason, against humanity and against good plain selfinterest. I think the opponents of immigration are suffering from a case of national myopia which is a very bad disease for a Canadian to have. There are people in this country who have homes, jobs, three meals a day and yet they say no more immigration. They are hopelessly wrong. If we are to listen to them we will be doing Canada a disservice which will be felt some day just as twenty-five years of very little immigration between the wars was felt in 1940 when we did not have enough hands to do the necessary jobs.
We have before us a unique opportunity. For the second time in a century we have the opportunity to populate this country on a large scale. We took advantage of the first opportunity before the first war. This is the second and probably the last opportunity that we shall have. We have already let six years slip away without fully taking advantage of the situation. But we have suddenly come to life. We have a selective planned immigration policy geared to our absorptive capacity. I endorse it, encourage it and support it, and I ask the government to keep them coming to this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask a question? You said we have a plan. Are you positive that this government has a plan, a sane immigration policy? Are you positive of that? I have never heard of it and they never have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am as positive of that as I can possibly be. I am satisfied that at the present time the government has a most excellent immigration plan. It is bringing people into this country, and the right kind of people. It may bring them in at the wrong time, but that is due to conditions that are very difficult to control. However, the over-all policy is a very sane one and the effect is being felt in Canada and appreciated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is it an adequate plan?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Keep quiet.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As to whether or not it is adequate, what I am saying to the house is, for the time being let us continue to bring them in at 200,000 or better a year, but certainly let us not cut that down. Getting back to immigration, I was saying that we had not taken full advantage of our opportunities. One does not know how much time there is left for immigration. One thing is certain. We will never build a greater Canada on lost chances. I want to make it clear that we cannot afford to lower our health and ideological standards. We only ask of the potential immigrant that he be sound physically and mentally, and by mentally sound I do not merely mean that he be sane but that he behave in a democratic manner, that he believe in democracy and conduct himself in a democratic fashion, that he keep his bargain with Canada, that he honour his commitment to go to work, and that he should make a bargain with himself to work harder in this country than he has ever worked before.
That is the kind of people we need. If he does that there is room for him in Canada, we want him, and he will become a good Canadian. No responsible person can advocate unlimited immigration. It would wreck the economy and social harmony in this country. But we cannot stand a cut-back at this time. To cut back on immigration is to cut back on our economic development. We have a glorious future in Canada which we can readily share with others. I think it will only be glorious if there are more and more people here with whom to share it. We are budgeting in this country for people as we budget for everything else. We are planning our Canadian family and we believe in large families. We need more Canadians. In order to have more Canadians we need more immigrants, and we need them now. I think the policy of the government is a wise one. I ask them to hold firm and to keep these immigrants coming. This country will be everlastingly indebted to them.
Since 1945 some of us in this house have been urging the government to do what they are now doing, and now we hear some rumblings in the country that they are going too fast. I say to the government: Do not believe it. There is ample and complete support for the present immigration policy. Let me close by reminding the house of something we know full well. Years ago Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that the twentieth century belonged to Canada. Like so many words of that great and far-seeing Liberal, this prophecy is coming true day by day. With half the
10, 1952
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale century over we find today that the world is our oyster. Our voices are heard in the councils of the world. Our prestige is high. On every side we hear our praises sung. We are fourth amongst the trading nations of the world and first on a per capita basis. Our standard of living is high, second only to that of the United States. Our finances are in excellent condition. Our diplomacy, exercised always in the interests of a cleaner and better world-the only kind of world in which Canada can flourish-has been masterfully handled by a statesman whose greatness is sometimes more fully recognized at the council tables of the world than here at home. I feel certain that my generation shares Sir Wilfrid Laurier's optimism. Our great need today is people and more people. I ask the government to keep them coming.
