I realize, Mr. Speaker, that entering the debate at this hour of the day is rather a difficult assignment, particularly when so many hon. members have folded their tents like the Arabs and silently stolen away. But I do want to take some part in the traditional debate on the speech from the throne.
Our session has been under way now for over a week. We have moved from the note of solemnity to a note of crisis, and now we are emphasizing the critical part of our discussion. As I look back at the debate which took place during the first three days of last week arising out of the foot-and-mouth disease crisis, I rather regret that I did not take some small part in that discussion; because as we consider the implications of that outbreak its ramifications become increasingly obvious. I must confess, however, that at that time foot-and-mouth disease was only a name to me. I must say I was greatly surprised to discover from the discussion that apparently very little was known of the details of that disease by those responsible for its control and elimination.
As the debate proceeded an old adage constantly recurred to me, which goes something like this.	For	the	want of a nail	theshoe was lost.	For	the	want	of	a shoe	thehorse was lost.	For	the	want	of	a horse	therider was lost.	For	the	want	of	a rider	the
battle was lost; and out of the loss of that battle a great nation entered into decline. It seemed to me that the negligence, which became increasingly obvious as the debate proceeded, is going to have very serious implications for the livestock industry of this country, and, as a matter of fact, has already had very serious consequences.

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale
From these few remarks I think hon. members will agree it is fairly obvious that I am still a comparatively new member of this house. It will be seen that I still place a little credence in the notion that governments are infallible, that governments do not make mistakes. From the layman's viewpoint that notion is cultivated today to an extent too great to be good for the political health of the nation; for the closer we come to the deliberations of this assembly the more we realize that the idol has feet of clay.
I would agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who said the other day that actually the government has no cure-all for the problems of the world. That becomes increasingly obvious the closer you get to the situation. Yet, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) earlier today, there has been an attempt to convey the impression, especially at election time, that governments are all knowledgeable, that governments are infallible-and particularly this government- when it comes to the handling of the social and political problems of the nation.
There is a real difficulty in cultivating public opinion today. It is a difficulty of communication, because the world with which we have to deal is largely out of reach, out of sight and out of mind. As a matter of fact, most of us are forced to look at a complex world by means of fixed images, or what we sometimes call stereotypes. Today these fixed images or stereotypes are readily established in the minds of the public through such means of communication as the press, the radio and the cinema, though they tell me that with the advent of television in the United States the politician is finding it increasingly difficult to befuddle the public. Television seems to have the happy faculty of getting to the character of the individual, and in the contact between the public and the politician it introduces an intimacy which is even closer than the contact made in the constituency itself, or when the politician is out stumping in connection with election activities. But up to the present it has been easy, by means of press, radio and cinema, to establish just the required impression in the thinking of the public; almost to manipulate public opinion in any desired direction.
If there has been any feeling that this government is infallible; if there has been any feeling that this government has a cure-all for the problems of the world, I would say that impression has been deliberately cultivated, particularly during election campaigns. Today governments do take much

credit for prevailing circumstances. Fortunately during this post-war period Canada has been riding the crest of an amazing wave of prosperity. I know the notion is abroad that what we experienced in Canada during and since the war has been the result of the benign, benevolent and progressive policies of the party in power. On the other hand, as an example-and this might also apply to other opposition groups-the party with which I am affiliated is almost synonymous with depression and everything that is bad for the health of the nation. I remember, for example, recently fighting the great battle of dates when an attempt was made to establish 1930 as the year in which the great depression began, though of course it is quite obvious that 1929 was the year of the onset of that depression. The reason for an attempt to establish the 1930 date of course is politically obvious. I believe we saw some of the same tactics in the speech delivered this afternoon by the member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). So assiduously and successfully has this attempt been made through the various media of communication I have mentioned that the opinion seems to be established that everything lovely in our present way of life is the direct product of government administration. For a time, I was under the impression that even the Almighty Himself had joined the government party. It was only last June that I had this opinion dissipated. Just before June 25 last, several members of the cabinet visited my constituency. I must say that we were honoured in having so many distinguished visitors. It became necessary to cover the constituency by airplane and give our message to the people by that method. I am told by one mother that, having heard a voice coming from the loud speaker in the airplane, her little girl rushed in and said, "Mother, God is telling everybody to vote for Mr. Dinsdale." Up to that point, I was under the impression the Almighty had abandoned us and joined the other side.
What is the real cause of the rather prosperous circumstances in which Canada finds herself at the moment? It is unexpected prosperity because all the experts, all the economists, were calculating for a recession immediately following the war. This condition results from such unexpected things as the backlog of demand, and perhaps more from the fact that during the war the centre of world influence, politically and economically, shifted from the old world and is now firmly lodged on this continent. This situation results also from the fact that during world war II

Canada was one of the great arsenals supplying all the material needs of modern warfare, and from the fact that in this country we have the richest resources of any nation in the world. This was effectively pointed out to us by the member for Calgary West (Mr. Nickle) in his maiden speech the other night. He gave us information concerning the development of the oil industry since 1947, particularly in Alberta, which was quite staggering and entirely new to most of the members in the house. Rather than give credit to any particular political regime for the situation in which Canada finds herself today, we should come to the conclusion that it is due to accidents of history and geography more than it is to deliberate government planning. After listening to the speech delivered a few minutes ago by the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), I am almost forced to the conclusion that had another group been in power Canada might have made greater strides, particularly in the field of immigration which supplies the basic ingredient for development in any country, namely human resources.
The situation is changing today. As we listened to the criticisms of the throne speech and of government policy-some of them have been quite effective-I felt that it was obvious that we are now in a period that might be referred to as a time of uneasy balance between the forces of inflation and those of deflation. For the first time since world war II the government is actually facing major difficulties. Yet there is still a spirit of easy optimism which perhaps is not justified by conditions that prevail in Canada today. From statements in the speech from the throne it would appear that that spirit of easy optimism still prevails in government circles. We find this statement in that speech:
At home our economy remains very buoyant. External trade and capital investment have reached record levels. Generally speaking employment remains at a high level. Inflationary pressures are still being strongly felt and require the maintenance of anti-inflationary measures.
This statement illustrates the easy optimism that has prevailed in Canada during these wonderful post-war years. Yet as we listened to the discussion today, I am sure there has been a growing feeling that the problems of inflation, which are closely connected with the problem of high taxation and the spreading unemployment, are not of merely transient significance. I think there are some deeper trends involved. I could go on, and I will later, to discuss farm problems, because the constituency I represent is basically an agricultural one.

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale
It is hardly necessary for me to deal in detail with inflation, high taxation and unemployment. Those subjects have been covered several times in the speeches today, but I should like to say that this feeling of buoyancy to which reference is made in the speech from the throne is more artificial than real. One of the common characteristics of inflation is that buoyant effect. In earlier periods when economies became completely bankrupt as a result of uncontrolled inflation, such occasions as the great south sea bubble, economies became so buoyant that they floated away. To say in these casual and easy terms that the economy remains buoyant, and refer to some of these major difficulties I have described, is to be rather overly optimistic at this time. Certainly the citizens of Canada on fixed incomes, the pensioners or recipients of war veterans allowance, would not concur in the idea that the economy is buoyant today.
I could dwell at length on some of the things that have come to my attention, particularly from the war veterans who are faced with the necessity of living on the meagre allowance permitted under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Changes in that act are to be considered during this session.
I only hope that the brief presented by the Canadian Legion will be seriously considered. I feel that the Canadian Legion, in all its presentations on behalf of the Canadian veteran, has demonstrated a spirit of responsibility and moderation, and obviously should be the group which is in closest touch with the needs of the ex-serviceman.
I would say that this deliberate psychological effect that the government has tried to cultivate in having the impression given that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds has been one of the biggest contributions to inflation. Quite often the economist, skilled in economics which is known among social scientists as the dismal science, makes gross errors in calculations because he refuses to recognize the influence of the psychological effect. In concealing, during times of special need, the facts of the situation and in suggesting that all is well and rosy in the garden and that everything will continue to be so under the best of all possible governments, there is cultivated an easy optimism in the thinking of the public, which makes it more difficult than it otherwise would be to deal with the effects of runaway or uncontrolled inflation. But notwithstanding that situation, we find that last year the standard of living remained the same as it was in 1950. There seems to have been a certain degree of self-control on the part of the consuming public. Connected with that fact, we must not forget the credit restrictions.

. The Address-Mr. Dinsdale It should be noted that the consumer saved twice as much in 1951 as he did in 1950. No doubt that fact too is associated with credit restrictions and might be described partly as a buyer's strike or a refusal to pay the prices demanded or the prices required as a result of the imposition of some of these excise taxes and hidden taxes that we have been discussing. Certainly I think the fact that the consumer has deliberately curtailed his expenditures and increased his savings gives the lie to the suggestion that the consuming public must be relieved of the surplus money it may have. We can come to no other conclusion than that this suggestion is made because the citizens of Canada are not to be trusted with the handling of their own hard-earned money. I say that the consuming public has given the lie to that statement by the record that has emerged from the statistical analysis for 1951.
As to taxation, we shall have plenty of opportunity to discuss that subject when the debate is taking place on the budget. I think it is significant, however, that the experts tell us that 25 per cent of a nation's income is a maximum for healthy taxation. Information has recently been given to the effect that on all levels of government, federal, provincial and local-that is, national taxation-has reached something like 40 per cent of the income, a fact which would tend to suggest that we have reached the point of diminishing return with regard to this method of gathering revenue for public expenditures. It is obvious that this is the situation. Time and again we have had it pointed out that initiative and productivity have been stymied as a result of the present policies of high taxation.
I am not going to dwell any longer on that point because it has been dealt with adequately already. I want to move briefly to a discussion of unemployment. That topic has also been mentioned on several occasions. I merely want to give a personal experience which occurred while I was in the city of Toronto just a week ago when I was invited there to take some small part in connection with the opening of education week. There I saw for the first time since the thirties a breadline consisting of some 200 men who were lined up outside a well-known church,
Woodgreen United Church, whose pastor is Rev. Ray McCleary; they were there for the purpose of receiving Sunday evening dinner. I was informed that this practice had been going on all during the winter. It was quite a shock to me, because it was the first time I had seen a breadline in Canada since the thirties and I happen to be one of the members of the depression generation who had some personal experience of the economic conditions prevailing during that period. With this easy attitude of optimism, this situation is passed off as a seasonal problem, and we are informed that everything will be well as soon as we take up the slack in our economy resulting from the dislocations which are inevitable as we move into an increased armament and defence program. We are told that as soon as that slack is removed, all will be well and all will be rosy in the garden again. We have had certain information brought before us by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) in dealing with unemployment in the textile industry. The information he placed on the record would tend to suggest that there is a threat of permanent unemployment in this one particular industry unless the government takes more drastic action than has been taken up to the present time.
I indicated that I wanted to say something about farm problems. This aspect has been discussed today, particularly by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). These matters have been forced upon our attention by the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease to which reference has already been made.
I am informed, Mr. Speaker, that the hour is now eleven o'clock. I should, therefore, like to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Dinsdale the debate was adjourned.
